Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to aerially seed areas of the fire that are critical to wildlife, or most at risk for long-term irreversible damage due to the effects of the fire. High elevation areas like the area targeted by this treatment often respond slowly following fire as their species are not fire tolerant. This opens the area up to non-native grass invasion. Sagebrush and yarrow were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to the treatment areas.\r\n\r\nEstablish one seeded plant per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide for watershed protection and reduce erosive potential.  Help provide cover and forage for wildlife.  Provide for soil stabilization on slopes and drainage bottoms.  Reduce potential for invasive weed introductions.  Provide browse for mule deer in crucial winter habitat.  Provide habitat for sage grouse and other birds and mammals that depend on sagebrush.
Planned_Implementation: Sagebrush and yarrow add vegetation structure and species richness to treated areas.  Aerially seed approximately 11,140 acres with Mountain Big Sagebrush and Western Yarrow.
Actual_Implementation: The aerial wildlife (high elevation) seeding was completed in January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  The aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct seed mix was dispersed over the targeted area at the specified rate.  The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Effectiveness Monitoring: BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites and to provide analysis on the general vegetation health of the burned area.

The Basco Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding applied was monitored at BAWH – 05 for three years and at BAWP – 01 for the second and final years. 
Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at low density at BAWH – 05: Western Yarrow was not recorded.  BAWP – 01 was initially established off-treatment in 2007 and had to be relocated during 2008 so no 2007 data exists for this plot. 
2008 – Mountain Big Sagebrush appeared to decline but remained at low density during the second monitoring season at BAWH – 05.  Minor fluctuations from year-to-year should be assessed cautiously because they may only reflect absolute non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  Western Yarrow was recorded at a high moderate density approaching the objective density of three plants per square meter at BAWP – 01; Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at low density. 
2009 – Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density.  During the second and final monitoring years, only one plant was recorded.  Western Yarrow was never recorded.  Mountain Big Sagebrush appears to be a difficult shrub to establish from seed: other applications of Mountain Big Sagebrush in the Elko District have met with low levels of success. The monitoring plot is located in a 10-12 inch precipitation zone where applications of Western Yarrow have generally been successful.  Reasons for the apparent lack of success of Western yarrow at BAWH – 01 are unknown.  Native release at BAWH – 01 was dense and combined a vigorous regenerating stand of Idaho Fescue in association with numerous broadleaf forbs including Arrowleaf Balsamroot.  Competition from native release may have inhibited establishment of seeded Western Yarrow (and Mountain Big Sagebrush) at BAWH – 01.  At BAWP – 01 Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density of two plants per square meter the first year, dropping to over one plant per square meter the second year.  Reasons for success of Western Yarrow at BAWP – 01 compared to apparent failure at BAWH – 01 are unknown.  BAWP – 01 is a floodplain site, BAWH – 01 a steep backslope. Because Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at BAWH – 01 during all three monitoring years, and exceeded the target density of one plant per square meter at BAWP – 01 during 2008 and 2009, we may consider the Basco Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding partially successful.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Human Life and Safety:  The burn area receives year round recreation use. Primary activities are off road vehicles, camping, hunting and target shooting. Visitor access may need to be controlled to ensure successful stabilization efforts and Public safety. Aircraft safety needs to be considered during aerial seeding operations.
   Soil/Water Stabilization: Need to reduce soil loss by wind and water erosion from exposed drainages and slopes and undesired transportation of soil particulate matter. Need to minimize loss of viable area seed bank, shrubs, perennial grasses and other native plant species from inevitable establishment and encroachment of annual invasives such as cheat grass, red brome and noxious weeds.
   Critical Heritage Resources:   Chaining operation will disturb the soil surface and could destroy Cultural Resources. Exposure
due to lack of vegetative cover could allow artifacts to be easily found and removed by the Public.
    Invasive Plants:  Areas subjected to wildfire are highly susceptible to entry of both noxious and invasive weeds. Cheatgrass and red brome are the invasive annuals of most concern within this area. Scotch and yellow star thistle are noxious weeds of concern within this burn area. Without aggressive measures to reestablish perennial plants, invasive annuals will dominate the site and the fire cycle will proceed on a short interval, excluding perennial vegetation from becoming established.

To enhance the herbaceous plant community by providing deeper rooted plants necessary for soil stabilization with the shrub and grass seed mix, to provide canopy cover, trapping snow and reducing evaporation from wind, and to reduce opportunities for increase of non-native, invasive species.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seed approximately 977 acres within a 2,960 acre area with mid-elevation aerial mix consisting of Basin Big Sagebrush, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and Western Yarrow.\r\nAerial seed approximately 977 acres within a 2,960 acre area with mid-elevation aerial mix consisting of Basin big sagebrush, Wyoming big sagebrush, Secar Snake River wheatgrass, and Western yarrow.  This seed mixture will be applied to the mid-elevation of the slopes.  Aerial seeding will be accomplished using a helicopter and seed bucket or broadcaster. The aerial seed will be applied when weather conditions are favorable to allow for coverage by snow or adequate moisture, and thus will be applied in late fall or early winter.
Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Mid-Elevation seed mixture included Basin Big Sagebrush, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Western Yarrow, and Snake River Wheatgrass.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Effectiveness Monitoring: 
The Aerial Midslope Seeding was monitored at seven locations; two specifically established for the treatment (CHWI – 01 and CHWI – 02), and five established to monitor other seedings that are overlapped by the Aerial Midslope Seeding (CHNB – 01, CHND – 01, CHND – 02, CHWC – 01, and CHWP – 01.) 
Monitoring Results:  
2006 – The midslope aerial wildlife seeding demonstrated poor success where monitored, with low rates of establishment for Western Yarrow and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Seeded grasses and Basin Big Sagebrush were not recorded.  Bluebunch Wheatgrass contributed to native release but most native release was low-growing Sandberg’s Bluegrass that survived the fire.  There was heavy growth of cheatgrass at the monitoring location. 
2007 – An additional sampling plot (CHND – 02) was established in 2007.  From 2006 to 2007, overall density of seeded species decreased by approximately 89 percent (CHWI – 01), and approximately 14 percent (CHWC – 01).  From 2006 to 2007 total density of native released species increased by approximately 76 percent (CHWI – 01). The increase in native release appears to be largely attributable to an increase in Sandberg’s Bluegrass bunches.  Seeded species establishment at CHWI – 02 appears to be more successful than at CHWI – 01.  This may be due to differences in soil conditions.  Native release establishment is not as significant at this site (CHWI – 02), but shows relatively high levels of species richness.  Severe drought conditions may be responsible for decrease in seeded species density (CHWI – 01).  
2008 – The aerial wildlife seeding on the Chance burn was monitored concurrently with other seedings where they overlapped.  Densities for both seeded and native release species declined for the aerial mid-elevation seedings during the monitoring period.  Snake River Wheatgrass was added to the aerial mid-elevation seeding mixture on the Chance burn: it exhibited very low rates of germination and establishment or was unrecorded at every monitoring plot.  Addition of grass to the aerial wildlife seed mixture was unusual, and (under conditions that prevailed throughout the period of germination and establishment) it appears to have been unjustified.  Overall success of the aerial wildlife seedings across the Chance burn varied with monitoring location but was generally poor.  No aerial seeded species were recorded or observed at CHNB – 01 during the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow established at low to moderate densities, demonstrating more success on water-receiving areas.  Basin and Wyoming Big Sagebrush germinated at very low densities: their eventual establishment as seeded species on the Chance burn is not assured.  The Chance aerial wildlife seedings may be rated partially successful based upon low to moderate establishment rates for Western Yarrow. 



CHWI-01
AERIAL MID-ELEVATION SEEDING
The Aerial Mid-Elevation seed mixture included Basin Big Sagebrush, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Western Yarrow, and Snake River Wheatgrass.  Snake River Wheatgrass was neither recorded nor observed at this location during the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow germinated at a density of near one-half plant per square meter, but declined to low density during the second year of monitoring, increasing slightly during the final year of monitoring.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at low densities during the first and final year of monitoring.  Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at low densities during the second and final year of monitoring.  
The Aerial Mid-Elevation Seeding was only partially successful at this location. All seeded species except the grass were recorded within quadrats.  Observation suggests Western Yarrow may be present at low to moderate densities on other parts of the slope.  Establishment and growth to maturity of seeded shrubs is not assured since they are present at such low densities.

CHWI-02
AERIAL MID-ELEVATION SEEDING
The Aerial Mid-Elevation seed mixture included Snake River Wheatgrass, Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, and Basin Big Sagebrush.  Snake River Wheatgrass was not recorded or observed during the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow germinated at a density of near one plant per square meter, increasing to more than one plant per square meter during the second year of monitoring and then declining to density below that recorded during the first year. Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at a low to moderate density of near one-third plant per square meter during the second year, declining to low densities during the final monitoring.  Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at low densities during the second and final year of monitoring.  
The Aerial Mid-Elevation Seeding was only partially successful at this location. All seeded species except the grass were recorded within quadrats.  Observation suggests Western Yarrow may be present at low to moderate densities on other parts of the ridgecrest.  Establishment and growth to maturity of seeded shrubs is not assured since they are present at such low densities.  

CHNB-01
AERIAL MID-ELEVATION SEEDING
The Aerial Wildlife seed mixture included Snake River Wheatgrass, Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, and Basin Big Sagebrush.  Snake River Wheatgrass, Western Yarrow, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush were neither recorded nor observed at this location.  Basin Big Sagebrush seedlings were not recorded but were observed at low densities outside quadrat frames along the paced transect.  The Aerial Wildlife Seeding was unsuccessful at this location.  Data gathered at this and other monitoring plots suggests that applying a ground or aerially broadcast seeding to an area with a dense, well-established, seral Sandberg’s Bluegrass/Hood’s Phlox vegetation complex invites failure because seeds are subject to competition from established vegetation.  Without pre-treatment disturbance of the soil surface, broadcast seedings of any kind should be restricted to areas that present a favorable seedbed, such as loamy sites with friable soil at the surface where fires have burned hot and reduced competition from pre-existing vegetation. 

CHND-01
AERIAL MID-ELEVATION SEEDING
The Aerial Mid-elevation seed mixture included Snake River Wheatgrass, Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, and Basin Big Sagebrush.  Western Yarrow was recorded at low densities until the third monitoring season, when it was not recorded.  Neither Wyoming Big Sagebrush nor Basin Big Sagebrush were recorded at any time during the monitoring period, but sagebrush seedlings of undetermined species were observed off-transect during the first year of monitoring.  The Aerial Mid-elevation Seeding was unsuccessful at this location.  
Data gathered at this and other monitoring plots suggests that applying an aerially broadcast seeding to an area with a dense, well-established, seral Sandberg’s Bluegrass/Hood’s Phlox vegetation complex invites failure because of competition with seeds from pre-existing vegetation.  Without pre-treatment disturbance of the soil surface, aerially broadcast seedings should be restricted to areas that present a favorable seedbed, such as loamy sites with friable soil at the surface where fires have burned hot and reduced competition from pre-existing vegetation. 

CHND-02
AERIAL MID-ELEVATION SEEDING
The Aerial Mid-elevation seed mixture included Snake River Wheatgrass, Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, and Basin Big Sagebrush.  Western Yarrow was recorded at consistent low densities during 2007 and 2008. Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Implementation of the proposed action described in the Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation Plan DNA for the Charleston Complex will protect soils in the burned area, including preventing potential loss of soil due to wind and water erosion&* will reduce potential invasion and establishment of noxious weeds and cheatgrass&* will provide quality forage for livestock and wildlife&* and will facilitate meeting established standards and guidelines for livestock grazing.  

Exclusion of livestock grazing is necessary to allow seedling establishment, restore plant vigor and seed production, and to allow reestablishment of preferred species and to deter invasion of undesirable species.  The proposed fence will be constructed around the burn perimeter to keep grazing animals off the recovering burn to allow establishment of seeded and pre-fire vegetation species.  This temporary fencing will be used in conjunction with existing fences to protect the burn area from grazing.  This fencing and subsequent rest from grazing will allow for plants to re-establish and develop effective root depths and root reserves.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of dust and ash storms decreasing visibility on Interstate 80.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of accelerated soil erosion and mud flows into Mary&$s River and other areas of concern and provide for soil stabilization.  Vegetation associated with wetlands, riparian zones, and floodplains will be allowed to reestablish. 

The broadcast seedings within drainages and low lying areas and aerial seeding on slopes will provide for soil stabilization and will reduce the potential invasion of cheatgrass, and any other nonnative noxious weeds.  The seedings will also provide cover and forage for area wildlife populations and nesting habitat for migratory birds.  Successful seeding of some drainages and the low lying areas near the South Fork of the Humboldt River and its tributaries will help reduce runoff and trap sediment, which will help prevent further degradation to the water quality.  Successful seeding of the drainages and low lying areas will also help protect aquatic species habitat from receiving excessive amounts of sediment and provide for streambank stabilization.

Control of noxious weeds is consistent with the management plans for the resource and will help protect the ecological integrity, biodiversity, and site productivity of this shrub-steppe plant community.  Treatment of noxious weeds is necessary to comply with Nevada State Laws, to implement the Integrated Weed Management Program of the Elko Field Office, and to be responsible neighbors to the adjacent private landowners.  Working cooperatively with local weed management groups and private landowners will achieve better weed management.

The proposed action conforms to the 1985 Wells Resource Management Plan (RMP), as it was amended for fire management on September 29, 2004.  The decision for fire rehabilitation from the Approved Fire Management Amendment, page 20, is to “Conduct fire rehabilitation activities to emulate historic or pre-fire ecosystem structure, functioning, diversity and/or to restore a healthy stable ecosystem.”  The proposed action is consistent with resource objectives of the plan and with other Federal, state, local and tribal laws, regulations, policies and plans to the maximum extent possible.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to seed watershed areas of the burn that are at highest risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion. Watersheds are especially at risk as they generally had the greatest build up of vegetation pre-fire, causing the fire to burn hot and destroy all vegetation and species in the seedbank. \r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Protect watershed areas from erosion.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 10062 acres with a watershed protection mixture (\u201cCharleston Watershed Mix\u201d) of \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and \u201cMagnar\u201d Basin Wildrye.\r\n\r\nAdd Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush to the watershed protection seed mixture (\u201cCharleston watershed mix\u201d) of native grasses.
Actual_Implementation:
Due to the availability of water and other resources necessary for regrowth, a mix of both native and non-native species (Snake River wheatgrass, Sherman big bluegrass, Magnar and trailhead Basin wild rye, Bluebunch wheatgrass, Siberian wheatgrass, Idaho Fescue, and Schwendimar and Bannock thickspike wheatgrass) was selected. Additional shrubs were added to the mix, and are discussed in the Burned Area Rehabilitation treatment monitoring section.

Implementation Monitoring:  
The aerial watershed protection seeding was completed during January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector.  AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct species seed mixture was dispersed over the targeted area at the specified rate. The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.

BAR addition of western yarrow and sagebrush:
“Delar” Small Burnet may have been substituted for Western Yarrow at some indeterminate locations. 
Because implementation was done concurrently with the aerial watershed protection seeding applied under emergency stabilization, only seed costs are reflected here.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding was monitored at seven separate locations (CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 06, CHWS – 07) specifically established to monitor this treatment on all range grazing allotments affected by the fire. 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  Basin Wildrye was also very successful
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, and CHWS – 05, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03.  Total seeded species density appeared to decline at CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 05, and CHWS – 07.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  All other seeded species declined dramatically and were not recorded, except at CHWS – 04, where Basin Wildrye was recorded at moderate density.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
The apparent disappearance of the majority of the seeded species of grasses during the second year of monitoring is problematic, and may be the result of a variety of causes.  Different technicians read the plots at different times of year between 2007 and 2008.  Seedlings may have become established the first year that later died off or went dormant because of persistent drought.  “Quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment may also have played a role: density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously.  Disappearance of most seeded species of grasses from the monitoring record the second year may not actually reflect their loss.  Data collected during the third monitoring year may help clarify these problems. 
2009 – Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 01 exceeded the target density by nearly four times.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 02 exceeded the target density by nearly five times.  Total seeded species density for CHWS – 03 approaches the target density, with Thickspike wheatgrass making the greatest contribution.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density for CHWS – 04 exceeds the target density by almost five times.  At CHWS – 05, only one specimen of Snake River Wheatgrass was recorded, other seeded species were not recorded.  At CHWS – 06, Thickspike Wheatgrass exceeded the target density.  At CHWS – 07 Basin Wildrye achieved a density of one and one-half plant per square meter during the final year: other seeded species were not recorded.  Abundant spring rains in later May and early June apparently benefited the establishment and success of this treatment with the monitoring period.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to seeded species density, exceeding the target density of three plants per square meter by four to five times at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 04.  The other seeded grass species appeared to return during the final year of monitoring, suggesting that their absence during 2008 only reflected dormancy and not extirpation.  Many previously unrecorded species appeared in the native release at monitoring sites across the treatment, also reflecting the abundant later spring precipitation.  “On average,” considering the extremely high densities recorded for Thickspike Wheatgrass at many of the monitoring locations and how well established many seeded species appear to be across the treatment, the Charleston Aerial watershed Protection Seeding should be considered fully successful. 

BAR addition:
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 and CHWS – 02, and appearing to decline slightly at CHWS – 03.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
Minor density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously: they may result from non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  At CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 total seeded species densities appeared to undergo steep declines.  Causes of opposite fluctuations in seeded densities between monitoring locations are unknown.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
2009 – Small Burnet went unrecorded during the final monitoring year.  It’s presence in the seed mixture was not uniform, and lack of record for the presence of the species the final year may be the result of “quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment.  Basin Big Sagebrush appeared to be well established at low to moderate densities at most monitoring locations by the close of the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density at CHWS – 03, but the species was “double seeded” at this location (as discussed in the analysis of the treatment above.)  At other locations Western Yarrow appeared well-established at low to moderate densities by the final year.  Basin Big Sagebrush and Western Yarrow were both recorded at low density at CHWS – 05. Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density and Western Yarrow was not recorded at CHWS – 07.  Results varied at the  numerous monitoring locations, but we may consider the addition of sagebrush and yarrow to the Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding partially successful. 
Regarding native release, reasons for the apparent precipitous decline in Sandberg’s Bluegrass density at CHWS – 03 from 2008 to 2009 are not known, but may reflect non-repeatability of individual quadrats along the paced transect.  Many previously unrecorded species were encountered at CHWS – 03 during 2009: they may have out-competed the Sandberg’s Bluegrass.  Alternately, the Prairie Junegrass and Kentucky Bluegrass identified during 2009 may have been previously misidentified as Sandberg’s Bluegrass.

Objectives: Establish ten firmly rooted desirable perennial plants per square meter (9.6 square feet) or 12% perennial cover within three years post-fire. The average frequency of non-native invasive annuals within the newly burned area should be less than twice what is found in an unburned reference area.
Planned_Implementation: This was the original aerial seeding mix.  El Aero Services was contracted to use a helicopter to fly on a mixture of perennial grasses and forbs. The seed was obtained from Stevenson Intermountain Seed Company, Wheatland West Seed LLC. Russell Barton, Granite Seed Company, Jimmy Goble, Eric Christensen, L & H Seeds, Inc. Brubakken and Reinbold, Inc., Native-Seed Company LLC, and Pawnee Buttes Seed, Inc. The seeds were tested. Following changes made to treatments from what was proposed in the ES plan, three different seed mixes were aerially applied to the Chrome Fire: the main aerial seed mix, the chaining seed mix, and the drill seed mix.
Actual_Implementation: Data from the final, close-out year show that the seeding treatments on the Chrome Fire have been fully successful. Seeded forbs Sanguisorba minor and Linum lewisii are abundant throughout the areas where they were seeded, as are the seeded perennial grass species (Tables 2, 4, and 6). Total perennial density is generally twice as high as firmly rooted perennials. This is due to seedlings from a variety of species continuing to establish. It is expected that not all of these seedlings will grow into mature, firmly rooted plants. Shrub density and cover has increased in the burned area over the three growing seasons post-fire. Newly established sagebrush seedlings have become more mature and larger plants. It is expected that overtime seeded forb species such as Sanguisorba minor will begin to fade out of the burned area as it returns to a community dominated by sagebrush and perennial grasses.\r\nInvasive annual grasses, mainly Bromus tectorum, are found only at low abundances within the burned area. However, they have increased over the three years of monitoring to at most 5-10 plants per square meter on average. This is much lower than most burned areas in the Ely District, and is still generally less than the unburned reference area (Tables 1, 3, and 5, Figure 1). Despite the increase over the three year period, it is unlikely that invasive annual grasses will increase in density above acceptable levels. The well established perennial plants should out-compete additional annual grasses and prevent a grass-fire cycle from occurring.\r\nIn addition to invasive annual grasses, a few other non-native weeds and one noxious weed (Carduus nutans) have become established on the Chrome Fire. While noxious Carduus nutans is only found at very low densities and not in any of the density subsamples, some non-native weeds are rather abundant within the Chrome Fire, especially Sisymbrium altissimum, Lactuca serriola, and Salsola tragus. These species can be found at 2-3 plants per square meter on average within many of the treatment areas. Halogeton glomeratus was also observed within a few density frames, but is found only at very low densities. However, it is likely that the well established perennial plants will out-compete these weeds. It is unlikely that these weeds will become a serious infestation within the burned area.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: After three growing seasons, the firmly rooted perennial plant objective has been met within all treatment types except the general aerial seed mix. The perennial cover objective has been met across all treatment areas. The non-native invasive annual objective has also been met; density of invasive annual grasses is lower on average within the burned area when compared to an unburned reference.

Objectives: 1. Limit the spread of invasive weeds, 2. Improve Soil Stability, 3. Increase native vegetation dominance and diversity, 4. Preserve watershed values and reduce erosion
Planned_Implementation: The seed was purchased at the October 2005 national seed buy in Denver, CO. The Non-wilderness PJ, wilderness PJ, and mesic blackbrush seed mixes were applied to the Duzak Fire during January and February of 2006. A BLM project inspector was on-site to ensure that the aerial seeding treatment was carried out appropriately and that unseeded control plots were not accidentally seeded. Shape files of seeded flight paths also indicate that seeding occurred in the appropriate areas, and did not occur in the designated controls.
Actual_Implementation:
Monitoring data after one growing season post-fire show the aerial seeding treatment on the Duzak Fire to not yet be effective. However, monitoring data from previous fires indicate that establishment of seeded species often takes more than one growing season. Success will be better determined in future years.
Methods: In June through August of 2006 Eastern Nevada Landscape Coalition Monitoring Crews collected data from a total of 270 macroplots. Ten of the brushbelt plots were used to monitor natural regeneration and were stratified by allotment and vegetation type, and were placed away from plots in the seeding treatments. The Mesic blackbrush mix was evaluated by comparing 40 seeded brushbelt plots with 39 unseeded control brushbelt plots. Additional coverage of mesic blackbrush seeding polygons was obtained with 132 additional aerial seeding plots. The non-wilderness PJ mix was evaluated by comparing 24 seeded brushbelts to 24 unseeded control brushbelt plots. Additional coverage of the non-wilderness PJ seeding polygons was obtained with 85 additional aerial seeding plots. The wilderness PJ mix was evaluated by comparing eight seeded brushbelts to eight unseeded control brushbelts. Additional coverage of the wilderness PJ seeding polygons was obtained with 10 additional aerial seeding plots
The brushbelt is a 5 X 30 m plot, adapted from the National Park Service’s Fire Monitoring Handbook. Within the brushbelt, intensive measures of density and cover by species is collected. Cover is measured along each edge of the brushbelt using an optical point projection device. Herbaceous and shrub seedling density is collected in ten, 0.5 square-meter density frames along these same transects. Shrub density is recorded from within the entire 5 X 30m brushbelt area. Additional species not found within the density frames or along the cover transects are searched for within the brushbelt and recorded. Paired replicates of seeded and unseeded control brushbelts are compared to evaluated treatment effectiveness.
The additional aerial seeding plot is a circular plot 30m in diameter used for obtaining better coverage of aerial seeding polygons. Within this plot, ocular cover estimates are recorded for species with 5% cover or greater, as well as for seeded species present Density measurements are recorded in 4, .5 square meter frames, where the focus is to search for establishing seedlings of seeded species.
All collected data was stored, cleaned, and analyzed using the Fire Ecology Assessment Tool (FEAT). Analysis provided by USGS-WERC consists of summary tables and means for seeded and naturally regenerating species separated by seeded and unseeded controls. Additional, more extensive analysis and reports will be provided by USGS-WERC during the winter of 2006/07.
Summary of Treatment Effectiveness: After one growing season, the aerial seed mix applied to the Delamar Fire has not yet been effective. In the Non-wilderness PJ mix seeding polygons, some seeded species are establishing are low densities including Poa secunda, Elymus elymoides, and Achnatherum hymenoides (Table 1). However, the density of these species is similar in both seeded brushbelts and unseeded control brushbelts, indicating that establishment may be due to natural regeneration rather than aerial seeding. In the Wilderness PJ Mix seeding areas, no seeded species were found in the density frames (Table 2). However, not enough data has been collected from these plots to adequately assess treatment effectiveness. More data from the Wilderness Mix in the Duzak Fire (approximately 20 more brushbelts and 40 more AA plots) will be collected towards the end of September, 2006. Results from this data should be available in a more extensive report scheduled for release in December, 2006. Achnatherum hymenoides, Sanguisorba minor, and Linum lewisii were found in the Mesic Blackbrush monitoring plots. Achnatherum hymenoides was found at a slightly higher density in the seeded brushbelts and additional aerial coverage plots than in the unseeded plots. It is uncertain if this is due to aerial seeding. The Sanguisorba and Linum are likely a result of aerially applied seed germinating.
One of the main purposes of the aerial seeding treatment is to reduce the abundance of invasive, non-native annual grasses. In both the Non-wilderness PJ mix seeding areas and Mesic Blackbrush Mix seeding areas, similar densities of exotic annual grasses are found in both seeded and unseeded control plots. These densities are also high (roughly 100 plants per square meter). Cover values may be reduced in seeded plots. Data from the Wilderness PJ Mix indicates higher densities in the seeded areas as compared to unseeded controls. Bromus establishment at higher elevations can often be patchy, and with the few plots so far sampled in this mix, patterns of Bromus establishment and dominance are still unclear. It is apparent that aerial seeding has so far been ineffective in reducing the establishment and abundance of invasive annual grasses.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: The treatment has not yet met its objectives. After one growing season, monitoring crews found seeded species establishing generally only at low densities in all three seed mix areas. The monitoring crews found similar densities of invasive annual grasses when comparing treated areas to unseeded controls. The success of the ground seeding treatment will be better assessed in future years since establishment of post-fire seeding often takes several growing seasons.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Implementation of the proposed action described in the Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation Plan EA for the East Humboldt Complex will protect soils in the burned area, including preventing potential loss of soil due to wind and water erosion&* will reduce potential invasion and establishment of noxious weeds and cheatgrass&* will provide quality forage for livestock and wildlife&* and will facilitate meeting established standards and guidelines for livestock grazing.  

Exclusion of livestock grazing is necessary to allow seedling establishment, restore plant vigor and seed production, and to allow reestablishment of preferred species and to deter invasion of undesirable species.  The proposed fence will be constructed around the burn perimeter to keep grazing animals off the recovering burn to allow establishment of seeded and pre-fire vegetation species.  This temporary fencing will be used in conjunction with existing fences to protect the burn area from grazing.  This fencing and subsequent rest from grazing will allow for plants to re-establish and develop effective root depths and root reserves.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of dust and ash storms decreasing visibility on Interstate 80.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of accelerated soil erosion and mud flows into the South Fork of the Humboldt River and its tributaries and provide for soil stabilization.  Vegetation associated with wetlands, riparian zones, and floodplains will be allowed to reestablish. 

The broadcast seedings within drainages and low lying areas and aerial seeding on slopes will provide for soil stabilization and will reduce the potential invasion of cheatgrass, Scotch thistle, hoary cress and Russian knapweed, and other invasive weeds.  The seedings will also provide cover and forage for area wildlife populations and nesting habitat for migratory birds.  Seeding with shrub and grasses will provide deep rooted perennial plants to establish, which will help provide soil stabilization, trap snow and reduce evaporation of the moisture from the soils due to wind.  Shrub establishment will also help the establishment of natural revegetation by capturing snow and providing moisture to grasses and forbs.  The shrubs will also provide sheltered areas from the wind, which will reduce some wind erosion on the site.  All of these functions enhance the herbaceous plant community which protects the soil form potential increased soil erosion that is likely following a fire and reduces the opportunities for increases in invasive nonnative plant or noxious weed species.  Establishment of vegetation helps to stabilize watersheds and upland soils to prevent further degradation to affected resources on lands within the fire perimeter or downstream drainages that may result from short duration, high intensity precipitation events.  Successful seeding of some drainages and the low lying areas near the South Fork of the Humboldt River and its tributaries will help reduce runoff and trap sediment, which will help prevent further degradation to the water quality.  The South Fork of the Humboldt River affected by the East Humboldt Complex supports important recreational fishing.  Successful seeding of the drainages and low lying areas will also help protect aquatic species habitat from receiving excessive amounts of sediment and provide for streambank stabilization.

Control of noxious weeds is consistent with the management plans for the resource and will help protect the ecological integrity, biodiversity, and site productivity of this shrub-steppe plant community.  Treatment of noxious weeds is necessary to comply with Nevada State Laws, to implement the Integrated Weed Management Program of the Elko Field Office, and to be responsible neighbors to the adjacent private landowners.  Working cooperatively with local weed management groups and private landowners will achieve better weed management.

The proposed action conforms to the 1987 Elko Resource Management Plan (RMP), as it was amended for fire management on September 29, 2004.  The decision for fire rehabilitation from the Approved Fire Management Amendment, page 20, is to “Conduct fire rehabilitation activities to emulate historic or pre-fire ecosystem structure, functioning, diversity and/or to restore a healthy stable ecosystem.”  The proposed action is consistent with resource objectives of the plan and with other Federal, state, local and tribal laws, regulations, policies and plans to the maximum extent possible.

Closeout Report:
$907,000 of the budgeted $1,025,000 was spent on the seed at the BLM Consolidated Seed Buy in Boise in Sept 2012. Two seed mixes were mixed at Ephraim. The seed purchase was the only BLM funding received for the entire Faust ESR Project.
Objectives: Perennial species at least 35% composition of the total plant community after the 3rd full growing season (2015) following the fire.\r\n\r\nThe species in the seed mix were selected with the focus on species that establish quickly, compete with cheatgrass, and stay green longer into the summer to make the seeded areas more resistant to fire and more tolerant of fire if the area burns again. The Faust West Hatch Ranch Seed Mix was designed for the soils and ecological sites on the west side of the Hatch Ranch road or the west side of the fire. The Faust East Hatch Ranch Seed Mix was designed for the remainder of the seeding treatments on the east side of the fire. The difference between these two areas is in effect elevation level, with higher elevation on the east side of the fire and in turn higher precipitation levels.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding followed by chaining with an Ely chain and drilling treatments would be\r\ncompleted this Fall, using a seed mix specifically prescribed for the ecological sites to\r\nstabilize the exposed soils of the fire. This treatment type would include 8,452 acres.
Actual_Implementation: Given the shortage of funding, only the highest priority areas were completed, which ended up being 4,064 BLM acres of aerial and chain (4,797 acres with state section), and 2,875 acres of drill seeding. The initial aerial seeding for the chaining area was completed on 12/19/12
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2015:
Drill seeding and aerial seed and chain treatments monitored at four locations have been successful. Composition of perennial species exceeded the 35% perennial composition objective. The 35% composition objective was measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial vegetation averaged approximately 46% for four monitoring locations.

FY 2016:
Drill seeding and aerial seed and chain treatments monitored at four locations continue to be successful. Composition of perennial species exceeded the 35% perennial composition objective. The 35% composition objective was measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial vegetation averaged approximately 55% for four monitoring locations.

PART 8- MONITORING RESULTS
Faust, G4Y3 - August 14, 2013
Response is based on elevation. Soils on the western end contain additional exchangeable sodium and calcium carbonate. The mid elevation and higher elevation soils are much improved containing more organic material and are much deeper soils. There is some growth of seeded species on the lower elevation drill seeding, but it needs more time to respond. A substantial amount of forage kochia and some seeded bunchgrasses were noted on these lower elevation sites. Natural reoccurring species are cheatgrass, tumble mustard, summer cypress and Russian thistle. Much of the mid elevation has a good response of native and introduced bunchgrass establishment. Some of the forage kochia and blue flax are also making inroads on these sites. The aerial seeded and chaining of the juniper stands occurring on the mid and upper elevations is providing very favorable results. Seeded species on these sites have frequent appearance. Notable growth of seeded species was observed for small burnett, Ladak alfalfa, blue flax, crested wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, Russian wildrye, and bitterbrush.

2015 Monitoring
Four sites (Sites #1, #3, #6, #8 listed above) were monitored on the Faust ESR on July 28 and August 11, 2015. Nested Plot Frequency transects were completed at all four sites. Both seeded material and volunteer plant material look very good. Drill seeding and aerial seed and chain treatments monitored at four locations have all been successful. Composition of perennial species exceeded the 35% perennial composition objective. The 35% composition objective was measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial vegetation averaged approximately 46% for four monitoring locations. Plant vigor is excellent at the chaining sites and the aerial seeding site. Species diversity is extensive throughout the treatment areas, but particularly impressive at the sites that were aerial seeded and chained. One site (AS#1) was monitored on the east side of the fire where no treatments occurred due to limited funding. This side of the fire did not burn as hot as the west side and perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs have re-established well. No noxious weed species were observed in the treatment areas. Monitoring results are documented below.
Livestock were present at the monitoring site in East Faust Creek and a salt block was nearby at the road. No other evidence of livestock use was observed. Wild horses from the Onaqui Mountain Herd were observed at lower elevations foraging outside the treatment areas on both the east and west sides of the fire. Several small bands were observed on the east side and one large band of 75 adults, plus foals was observed on the west side.

2016 Monitoring
Four sites were monitored on the Faust ESR between June 20th and 23rd, 2016. Nested Plot Frequency transects were completed at all four sites. Both seeded material and volunteer plant material look very good. Drill seeding and aerial seed and chaining treatments monitored at four locations have all been successful. Composition of perennial species exceeded the 35% perennial composition objective. The 35% composition objective was measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial vegetation averaged approximately 55% for four monitoring locations. Plant vigor is excellent at both chaining sites and the aerial seeding site on the east side. Species diversity continues to be extensive throughout the treatment areas. Dalmatian toadflax was observed on one of the chaining treatment areas and exceeds the noxious weed objective. Monitoring results are documented below.
All fences, gates, and cattleguards around the aerial seed and chaining treatment area are intact and in good condition. Evidence of livestock use was observed in East Faust Creek, with little to no impact on aerial seeding treatment in that area. No other evidence of livestock use was observed in treatment areas. The Onaqui Mountain Wild Horse Herd was observed frequently in late spring and periodically through summer months at lower elevations in the drill seeding area.

Objectives: The primary objective is to aerially seed burned areas to provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.  Kochia was chosen to add vegetation structure and species richness to the burn.  Seeded areas cover locations at greatest risk for damage from fire effects, including soil erosion and weed invasion.  \r\nEstablish one seeded Kochia half-shrub per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 2993 acres with Forage Kochia.
Actual_Implementation: The aerial wildlife seeding was completed in January via helicopter through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Gopher Aerial Kochia Seeding was monitored at two widely separated locations (GOWK – 01 and GOWK – 02). 
Monitoring Results:
2007 – At GOWK – 01 Forage Kochia was recorded at low moderate density near one-third plant per square meter: Winter Wheat was not recorded.  At GOWK – 02 Forage Kochia was recorded at very low density: Winter Wheat was not recorded. 
2008 – At GOWK – 01 Forage Kochia appeared to decline to a low density.  Small fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously because past the first photographed quadrat, individual frames along a paced transect are not perfectly repeatable from year to year.  At GOWK – 02 Forage Kochia was not recorded.  Winter Wheat was not recorded at either monitoring location but would not have been expected to persist into the second year.  
2009 – At GOWK – 01 Forage Kochia appeared to increase slightly but remained at low density.  At GOWK – 02 Forage Kochia was recorded at very low density.  Winter Wheat was not recorded at either monitoring location.  Based upon consistent (though fluctuating) presence of Forage Kochia throughout the monitoring period at both widely separated monitoring locations we may consider the Gopher Aerial Kochia Seeding to be partially successful.  Caution suggests we regard this seeding as only marginally successful.  At GOWK – 01 conditions were very weedy, especially during the first two years of the monitoring period.  The paced transect that monitored the treatment proceeded from a weedy exposed ridgecrest into a protected swale.  By the end of the monitoring period most recorded Forage Kochia plants were encountered toward the end of the transect in the area protected from wind.  Wind action appears to have redistributed Kochia seed near GOWK – 01.  Reasons for the low level of success of this treatment at GOWK – 02 (a protected toeslope and prehistoric floodplain) are less clear.

Objectives: Establish 2 or more firmly rooted, desirable perennial plants per 9.62 square feet or 6% desirable perennial cover. The average frequency of non-native invasive annuals within the newly burned area should be approximately equal to the seeded portion of the Gregerson Complex burned/unburned reference area.
Planned_Implementation: El Aero Services was contracted to use a helicopter to fly on a mixture of perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs. The seed was obtained from the regional warehouse in Boise, Idaho and from the Ely seed warehouse. The seeds were tested.
Actual_Implementation: After three growing seasons, invasive grasses are pervasive in the burned area and perennial plants are regenerating well. On average, there are close to 300 plants per square meter of Bromus tectorum and Bromus rubens (Table 1 and Figure 1). Invasive annuals are actually lower post-fire within the reference area that burned by the 2005 Delamar Fire. The 2005 growing season was preceded by an abnormally wet winter and spring, fueling a bumper crop of invasive annual grasses. The 2007 growing season was preceded by a relatively dry winter and spring hindering invasive annual establishment.\r\nDespite the dominance by invasive annual grasses, perennial plants are regenerating quite well within the Gregerson Burned Area, especially grasses. This is due primarily to three species that are establishing naturally post-fire: Elymus elymoides at nearly one plant per square meter on average, Elymus lanceolatus at nearly two plants per square meter on average, and Pleuraphis jamesii at nearly one plant per square meter on average.\r\nPerennial forbs are less common on average than perennial grasses within the burned area, but still make up an important group at over 2 plants per square meter on average. The most common species are Spheralcea ambigua, Phlox longifolia, and Machaeranthera canescens. The data show a sharp decline from 2005 to 2006 in average perennial forb density. This may be due to shifting plot locations rather than a real decline.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: After three growing seasons, the firmly rooted desirable perennial plant objective has been met on the Gregerson Fire. Density and cover of invasive annual grasses on the Gregerson Fire are much higher when compared to the adjacent unseeded portions of the 2005 Delamar Fire.

Objectives: Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. Seeding occurred on sites that do not have the likelihood of naturally recovering from the fire. Areas were seeded with perennial species to reduce the dominance of Bromus tectorum. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.

Objectives: The objectives for cover will be to obtain 70% of all perennial plant cover found in the associated reference site, or, when not possible, achieve 50% of the lowest value for perennial cover associated with the appropriate ecological or range site by the need of the third year. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding was vital in mitigating the potential loss of Greater sage grouse habitat in the Montana, Granite, and Bilk Creek mountain ranges. Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the Greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. The areas selected are predominantly upland areas where topography is unsuitable for drill seeding due to slope and accessibility. All aerial seeding occurred in sage grouse PPH or PGH that was severely burned. Sage grouse habitat in the Bilk, Trout Creek, and Montana Mountains is widely regarded as being exceptionally productive when compared with other areas designated as sage grouse PPH. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land.
Actual_Implementation: Original ESR-funded aerial contract was for 45,284 acres. Since contract bid was based on pounds of seed, not acres, some leftover seed from original project (avoided unburned islands) was used to increase treatment area with ESR funds. Nevada Dept. of Wildlife, Ruby Mitigation Fund, and NGO private contributors also contributed seed and aircraft time to increase accomplishments.

Actual_Implementation:
On 4 January 2002, day 1, the BLM aerial seeding crew started the rangeland seeding on the 2001 Hot Lake Fire. On site was one EI Aero helicopter with pilot (Ted McBride), and fuel truck with fueler. EI Aero also supplied the seed mixer and two seed buckets. BLM supplied five ground crew members and one project inspector (Tyson Gripp). Also on site was one member from Germn-8, who treated all the seed with a fertilizer to increase germination in the seed. Start time was 1300. We started so late because the seed truck got stuck in the snow and mud and we had to get a grader from the Normandy Mine to pull it out. We seeded off the Scraper Springs intersection instead on the Red Road because of the road conditions. The weather was sunny with highs in the low 40's.
Started the winter deer seeding which included Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush, western yarrow, and forage kochia. Finished the rest of the day at 1630 with 1,060 lbs. of winter deer wildlife seed on the ground. Day 2, January 5, 2002, started at 0830. It started snowing at 1030 which grounded the helicopter until 1145. We started seeding again, but the snow grounded us at about 1345. Had to stop the job completely for the day at 1600 again because of the snow. Ended the day with 5,290 lbs. of seed on the ground. Day 3, January 6, 2002, start time was 0800. Fresh snow had covered all of the seed that we had put out the prior two days proving protection from seed loss from wind and animals. By mid day it started raining melting the snow moderately. The final for the day was 7,280 lbs.. Total aerial Rock Creek Gorge North Critical Deer Winter Wildlife Seeding consisted of 13,630 lbs. of seed at 2.9 lbs./acre, over 4,590 acres.

On February 2, 2002 the Hot Lake Fire Rock Creek Gorge South Critical Deer Winter Wildlife Aerial Seeding was began. The seeding was done via rental agreement with EI Aero. EI Aero was used because Silverhawk was not available at the time as was initially planned. EI Aero supplied a helicopter and pilot, two seed buckets, fuel truck with crew and seed mixer. BLM
supplied the ground crew ( five people) and one project inspector.
The seed mix called for on the project was: 1,622 lbs. Wyoming Big Sagebrush, 6,891 lbs. Basin Big Sagebrush, 6081bs. Western Yarrow and 5,270 lbs. Forage Kochia. There was no GermN8 treatment on this project as per Tom Warren, Seeding was done on every other swath. On the lower elevations there was a snow coverage of approximately 0 to 50% increasing to total coverage at the higher elevations. Seeding began at approximately 0900 at the higher elevations along the ridge to the north. I went out on an ATV to inspect. I observed an even flow from the seed bucket and good even seed distribution in the snow on the ground. I paced several swath widths which were averaging 80 feet. The day&$s total was 9,900 lbs. of seed covering 2,830 acres yielding 3.5 lbs./acre.
On February 3, 2002 seeding resumed. The helicopter was moving toward the lower elevations to the south. Again I went out on an ATV and observed an even flow from the bucket and good even seed distribution in the snow. Again the swaths averaged 80 feet when paced. I also observed that the bare ground at lower elevations ranged from moist to muddy from the snow melt. Along the edges of the burn there were numerous fingers and islands of sage going into the seeding area. The day&$s totals were 3,945 lbs. of seed covering 1,072 acres yielding 3.68 lbs./acre. The Rock Creek Gorge South portion was finished at 1100. The totals for the project were 13,845 lbs. of seed covering 3,902 acres yielding 3.55 lbs./acre as the treatment called for.

Objectives:
The aerial seeding treatment will be deemed effective if the following objectives are met. 1)
An average of three desirable perennial plants per square-meter will be permanently
established in the burned area within three growing seasons post-fire. 2) The seeding will
result in greater abundance (density and cover) of seeded species when compared to
unseeded controls. 3) The seeded area will have lower abundance (cover) of invasive annual

pulled from the drill mix because they have shallower planting depth requirements than the
remainder of the drill mix and will be more successfully seeded by an aerial application.
Additional seed species that are beneficial to sage grouse will be contributed by the Nevada
Department of Wildlife (NDOW).

Aerial seeding was completed via a Call-When-Needed
helicopter contract with El Aero Services and was staffed by
Ely ESR and fire crew. The ES and BAR seedings took place
in 2 phases due to delayed seed delivery timelines. The
Emergency Stabilization sage grouse mix was applied the 2nd
week of December and the Burned Area Stabilization mix was
applied when seed was delivered in January 2015. Seed was
mixed onsite by Ely ESR staff and BLM fire crew. Monitoring
data for FY15 will be available in October of 2015 after data
entry and analysis have been completed.

Actual_Implementation: Even though this burn did not achieve its perennial recovery objective of 25% cover, natural revegetation was successful. The success of this burn indicates how unrealistic the objective is of 25% perennial cover after only three growing seasons. Unrealistic recovery objectives is a recurring theme in older fire plans. Currently, the Ely Office ESR program is working to have more attainable recovery objectives. Unlike several other 2001 burns in White Pine County, this burn was not heavily invaded by Halogeton glomeratus or Salsola kali, which facilitated the success of the treatment. The lower densities of Halogeton glomeratus or Salsola kali may have been partially due to the remoteness of the burn. Some erosion was present on the burn especially along the road; road maintenance may be needed in the future if water erosion continues. Erosion within the burn is not a major concern with the high level of perennial establishment.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to aerially seed areas of the fire that are critical to wildlife, or most at risk for long-term irreversible damage due to the effects of the fire. Anatone bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue and Basin big sage were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to the treatment areas.\r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerially seed approximately 1,929 acres with a low elevation wildlife mixture of Idaho Fescue, “Anatone” Bluebunch Wheatgrass, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  

•	Lower elevation on 1,570 acres.  The seed mix is Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush Bannock cultivar), thickspike wheatgrass and Western yarrow.

Acres treated will be seeded aerially based on ecological site potentials with the use of a helicopter with a seed broadcast bucket.  Seeding in swaths (e.g. seed application on 80 foot swath, leave 160 foot swath and apply again) that allow for plant establishment and future seed sources will be prioritized on any “large” areas that burned completely.  Selective spot seeding will also be considered due to the mosaic of vegetation types affected and to avoid intact unburned areas to where specific sagebrush species will be seeded considering site potential.  Acreage would be duplicated on those areas where aerial seeding and on-ground antelope bitterbrush seeding occurs on the same affected site.  Bluebunch wheatgrass might be substituted with Snake River wheatgrass, a native perennial species.

Seed mixtures shown in this subsection would allow for additional rehabilitation of wildlife habitat as well as allow watershed protection and reduce erosion potential.  The consideration of acreage seeded includes, 1) two-tracks for potential vegetated fuel breaks separate from this DNA, 2) private lands and 3) the estimated unburned areas within the perimeter. The seeding would provide cover and forage for at least 250 wildlife species that inhabit sagebrush habitats and interspersed riparian/meadow habitat including sage grouse and mule deer, migratory birds and Special Status Species.  It would also provide vegetation needed for ecological site dynamics.
Actual_Implementation: Anatone bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue and Basin big sage were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to the treatment areas.\r\n\r\nThe aerial wildlife seeding was completed in January by helicopter through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

Monitoring Results: 
2007 –Bluebunch Wheatgrass was also seeded at MUBB – 01 with the Aerial Watershed Protection seeding (“double seeded”) and so an absolute determination of seeding success by treatment cannot be made for this monitoring location.  At MUBB – 01 total seeded species exceeded the objective density of three seeded plants per square meter, with Wyoming Big Sagebrush making the greatest contribution. 
2008 – At MUWD – 01 Idaho Fescue was recorded at a density of near one and one half plant per square meter. 
2009 – At MUWD – 01 Idaho Fescue was recorded at a density of over one plant per square meter.  At MUBB – 01 Bluebunch Wheatgrass was recorded at a density approaching one-half plant per square meter, but it was “double seeded” at this location, as mentioned above.  The presence of seeded species at both monitoring locations at low moderate or moderate densities during the final year of monitoring allows us to rate this seeding as partially successful.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The Neck Fire (BIEH) began on July 21,2005 and was contained on July 24, 2005. The fire burned 4,931 acres in the Black Hills, approximately 25 miles northeast of Cedar City, Iron County, Utah. The area is habitat for southwest desert big game populations (mule deer and antelope), Utah prairie dogs, and sage grouse. Over 90% of the fire occurred within the Adams Well and Lowe allotments, with small portions of the fire crossing fences into the Minersville #5 and Nada allotments. Approximately 4,138 acres of federal and 793 acres of state managed pinyon juniper woodlands and sagebrush/grasslands were consumed by the fire. This was a typical wind driven fire that burned rapidly and with great intensity, consuming the canopy of the trees as well as the sparse understory vegetation. In the sagebrush/grasslands the fire burned with less intensity and moved much slower being carried by cheatgrass.
