Objectives: To establish one to three seeded shrub plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment; to provide watershed protection and reduce erosion; to enhance site stabilization, trap snow and reduce evaporation; and to provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species and migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 302 acres with Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Basin Big Sagebrush, and Western Yarrow.\r\nBroadcast seed approximately 302 acres for wildlife habitat with Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush.  In order to help Wyoming and basin big sagebrush to re-establish within the burn, it is proposed to aerially seed the public acres (895) of the fire, every third 60 foot swath with the two sagebrush species and Western yarrow.  Seeding every third swath would actually seed approximately 302 acres.  Treatment would be completed using a helicopter and bucket.  Seed would be applied when weather conditions are favorable to allow for coverage by snow or adequate moisture, and thus would be applied in late fall or early winter.
Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Wildlife Protection seed mixture included Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Basin Big Sagebrush, Basin Wildrye, Thickspike/Streambank Wheatgrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, Big Bluegrass, and Canby Bluegrass.  The addition of multiple species of grasses to the aerial wildlife seeding on the Oyster burn was unusual.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The Oyster Aerial Wildlife Seeding overlapped the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding and the drill seedings, so was monitored concurrently at plots established for monitoring the other seedings. 
(OYWP-01) 
AERIAL WILDLIFE SEEDING
The Aerial Wildlife Protection seed mixture included Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Basin Big Sagebrush, Basin Wildrye, Thickspike/Streambank Wheatgrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, Big Bluegrass, and Canby Bluegrass.  The addition of multiple species of grasses to the aerial wildlife seeding on the Oyster burn was unusual.  Western Yarrow, Basin Wildrye, and Thickspike/Streambank Wheatgrass, were seeded twice (“double-seeded”) at this location: once with the native drill seeding and once with the aerial wildlife seeding.  Discrimination of which seedlings were established from what treatment is not possible.  Densities for these seeded species were not divided, but were considered in total within the context of each treatment.  
Western Yarrow germinated at low density, declined to very low during the second monitoring season, and appeared to increase back to a low density of a little over one-third plant per square meter during the final year.  Fluctuations such as this can be deceptive and may result from the non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush germinated at very low density, increasing to low density during the second year and appearing to decrease slightly during the final year.  Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density during the second season of monitoring, increasing to a low density of one-fifth plant per square meter during the final year of monitoring.  
Total seeded grasses germinated at low density (only 4 individuals were recorded), then appeared to disappear entirely during the second two years of monitoring. 
The Aerial Wildlife Seeding was unsuccessful at this location.  Total seeded species never achieved the objective density of from one to three plants per square meter.  Only Western Yarrow had achieved moderate densities by the final year of monitoring, but all seeded species had generally increased on the site during the monitoring period.  Yarrow seems likely to persist at this location.  The slowly increasing densities suggest likely future establishment of the seeded sagebrush subspecies on this site.  

(OYBB-01) 
AERIAL WILDLIFE SEEDING
The Aerial Wildlife Protection seed mixture included Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Basin Big Sagebrush, Basin Wildrye, Thickspike/Streambank Wheatgrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, Big Bluegrass, and Canby Bluegrass.  The addition of multiple species of grasses to the aerial wildlife seeding on the Oyster burn was unusual.  Western Yarrow was not recorded during the first year, appeared at moderate density approaching one-half plant per square meter the second year, and increased to over three-quarters plant per square meter during the final year of monitoring.  Western Yarrow, Thickspike Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, and Big Bluegrass were seeded twice (“double-seeded”) at this location: once with the native drill seeding and once with the aerial wildlife seeding.  Discrimination of which seedlings were established from what treatment is not possible.  Densities for these seeded species were not divided, but were considered in total within the context of each treatment.  It is probable but not certain that the double-seeded species that became established originated with the drill treatment and not the aerial treatment at OYBB – 01.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was neither recorded nor observed at this location.  Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded during the second season of monitoring (only) at very low density.  Seeded grasses germinated at a low density of about one-quarter plant per square meter, then increased during the second year to a moderate density exceeding one plant per square meter, then decreased to under one-third plant per square meter during the third year.  The increase of seeded grass density during the second year of monitoring may be attributable to particularly favorable timing of spring precipitation during that year (2007). 
The Aerial Wildlife Seeding was partially successful on this site based upon increasing moderate densities of Western Yarrow.  Yarrow seems well established and likely to persist at this location.  The future establishment of the sagebrush subspecies seeded on this site is uncertain. 

(OYND-01)
AERIAL WILDLIFE SEEDING
The Aerial Wildlife Protection seed mixture included Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, Basin Big Sagebrush, Basin Wildrye, Thickspike/Streambank Wheatgrass, Bluebunch Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, Big Bluegrass, and Canby Bluegrass.  The addition of multiple species of grasses to the aerial wildlife seeding on the Oyster burn was unusual.  Western Yarrow, Thickspike Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, and Big Bluegrass were seeded twice (“double-seeded”) at this location: once with the native drill seeding and once with the aerial wildlife seeding.  Discrimination of which seedlings were established from what treatment is not possible.  Densities for these seeded species were not divided, but were considered in total within the context of each treatment.  It is probable but not certain that the double-seeded species that became established originated with the drill treatment and not the aerial treatment at OYND – 01.  Western Yarrow germinated at a moderate to high density of almost four and one-half plants per square meter, declining to over three plants per square meter in the second year of monitoring, and to under three plants per square meter in the final year.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush germinated at low density, declined to very low density during the second year, then appeared to increase during the third year.  Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at low density during the second year (only). 
Total seeded grasses germinated a high density of about three and one-half plants per square meter, decreased during the second year to a density of about two and one-half plants per square meter, finally increasing to about two and three-quarter plants per square meter during the third year.  Reasons for the decline in density of seeded grass after the first year are unknown.  
The Aerial Wildlife Seeding was partially successful on this site based upon increasing moderate densities of Western Yarrow.  Conclusions drawn from yarrow densities should be regarded with caution however, since the species was double-seeded and the drilled and aerially broadcast components of the total seeded yarrow applied at OYND – 01 cannot be separated.  Yarrow seems well established and likely to persist at this location.  The future establishment of the sagebrush subspecies seeded on this site is uncertain. 

Monitoring Results:  
2006 – The aerial wildlife seeding was monitored at all three plots on the Oyster burn. Interpreting density data for the aerial wildlife seeding is problematic where sampled at monitoring plot OYND – 01 because Thickspike Wheatgrass, Big Bluegrass, and Snake River Wheatgrass were seeded twice (“double-seeded”) at this location: once with the native drill seeding and once with the aerial wildlife seeding.  Discrimination of which seedlings were established from what treatment is not possible.  Densities for these seeded species were not divided, but were considered in total within the context of each treatment.  It is probable but not certain that the double-seeded species that became established originated with the drill treatment and not the aerial treatment, at OYND – 01.  Success of the aerial wildlife seeding seemed greatest at OYND – 01, poor at the other drilled seeding monitoring site (OYBB – 01), and poorest at the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding monitoring plot (OYWP – 01).   These numbers should be interpreted with caution for OYND – 01 because of the double-seeding at that location.  Native release was very good at OYWP – 01, and may have out-competed the aerial wildlife seeding.  Sagebrush establishment was not good on any monitoring plot, with no individuals of Basin Big Sagebrush recorded.  There is little or no cheatgrass on the Oyster burn. 
2007 – Total seeded species density decreased by approximately 34 percent at OYND – 01, and by approximately 26 percent at OYWP – 01, reflecting decreases in grasses, forbs, and shrubs at both sites: seeded grasses were not recorded.  At monitoring plot OYBB – 01 total seeded species density increased by 458 percent, reflecting increases in both seeded grasses and Western Yarrow.  Total native release species density increased by approximately 6 percent at (OYND – 01), 6 percent at (OYWP – 01), and 47 percent at (OYBB – 01).  Increases include increases in individual species densities and increased native release species richness.  Reasons for the general increase in native release across the Oyster burn from 2006 to 2007 are unknown but may include favorable timing and amount of precipitation that fell during spring of 2007.  This does not explain the concurrent decrease in seeded species, unless the increased competition from native release vegetation suppressed germination and establishment of seeded species. 
2008 – Success of the aerial wildlife seeding varied from plot to plot, and may be assumed to have been patchy throughout the burn.  Total seeded species density decreased from 2007’s high at OYBB-01, with grasses decreasing and forbs increasing.  Total seeded species density also showed minor decrease at OYND – 01, with grasses increasing slightly, and forbs and shrubs decreasing slightly.  These changes may or may not be significant.  At OYWP – 01 total seeded species increased, reflecting increases in Western Yarrow only: seeded grasses were not recorded for the second year in a row.  Total native release species density remained relatively constant at OYND – 01, increased at OYWP – 01 reflecting increases in Green Rabbitbrush, At OYBB – 01 native release declined overall, but fluctuations may represent sampling “artifacts” resulting from non-repeatability of individual quadrats along the paced transect.  Western Yarrow dropped below the objective density at OYND – 01 during 2008.  At the other monitoring locations, seeded species never achieved the objective densities of three seeded plants per square meter.  The aerial wildlife seeding may be considered partially successful based upon moderate densities of Western Yarrow established at OYND – 01 during the final monitoring year.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The purpose of the proposed action described in the emergency stabilization and rehabilitation plan and this EA is to protect the burned area from livestock grazing, seed the burned area to stabilize the soils and prevent the establishment of annual, invasive nonnative plant species, and noxious weed species, allow the undamaged plant species time to re-establish, and treat the invasive nonnative plant and noxious weed species to prevent spreading.  The need for the proposed action is to stabilize and prevent unacceptable degradation to natural and cultural resources, to minimize threats to life or property resulting from the effects of the fire, and to construct physical improvements necessary to prevent degradation of land or resources.  To prescribe cost effective post-fire stabilization measures necessary to protect human life, property, and critical cultural and natural resources.  Monitoring the proposed action for the burned area and adjacent unburned areas is needed to document the results of the proposed action and necessary for the management of the public lands.\r\n\r\nThe proposed seeding would help stabilize the watershed to prevent further degradation to affected resources on lands within the fire perimeter or downstream drainages that may result from short duration, high intensity precipitation events&* reduce the potential for invasive nonnative weeds and competitive annual plant species&* help provide forage, cover, and habitat for wildlife, including but not limited to species such as, BLM designated special status species, migratory birds, mule deer, pronghorn antelope, and sage grouse.

Objectives: The objectives are to stabilize the soils in the aread of moderate to high burn intensity (areas that supported Pinyon/Juniper) and to help restore wildlife habitat.
Planned_Implementation: The area would be aerial seeded using a rotor wing aircraft of 1371 acres.  Seed will be applied at a rate of 12.3 bulk pound per acre of native seed mix.  Seeding would be done during the winter of 2002/2003.
Actual_Implementation: Of the seeded species, Sherman big bluegrass (Poa secunda), magnar basin wildrye (Elymus elymoides), mountain big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata var. vaseyana), and four-wing saltbrush (Atriplex canescens) were seen to have emerged. All of these did well on the north facing slope plot, while only Sherman big bluegrass (Poa secunda) emerged on the south facing slope plot.\r\n   Only two plots were located on the burn. This gave little understanding of the vegetation distribution of the entire area. We believe this is resulting in sampling error that is causing our data to be so extreme. It is difficult to make judgments based on only two plots which show completely different results. More monitoring sites need to be initiated during the first year after treatment so that a more comprehensive and accurate view of the revegetation is documented.\r\n   One interesting note is that on both plots shrubs did not really begin to establish until year 2. On average, in both cover and density estimates, shrubs increased in year two and further increased in year 3. This is just another indication that shrub seedlings may not emerge for a year, or two or three after seeding and that closure to grazing continues to be important after the third year of ESR funding and monitoring.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Two monitoring study areas established in aerially seeded area; seeded species establishment on study area #1 is virtually nonexistent, but moderate to good in the study area #2. Study area #1 was located on a south facing slope and dominated by the invasive annual grass, Bromus tectorum, with a little growth from natives such as Poa secunda, Stipa comata, and
Ephedra viridis. Study area #2 was located on a north facing slope, had very little Bromus tectorum and was mostly dominated by natives such as Agropyron spicatum, Agropyron trachycaulum, Atriplex canescens, Argemone sp. and Artemisia tridentata vaseyana. Seeded species had good success on this north facing slope. It is uncertain whether this was due to lack of
cheatgrass, more moisture or a combination of both. However, the difference between study area #1 and #2 was dramatic.
   The objective of 3-5 perennial grass or shrub plants/m2 was taken from IM 84-256, in which this amount was required in order to obtain a Rangeland Condition Class of “Good” for a range area. Seeding success was determined by the average 3-5 seeded grass or shrub plants/m2 estimated through monitoring. The objective of 3 seeded grass or shrub plants/m2 was taken from IM 84-256, in which this amount was required in order to obtain a Rangeland Condition Class of “Good” for a seeded area
   In summary, the treatment did not meet revegetation objectives and showed a lack of seeded and total grass/shrub density after the three years. Data collected showed that seeded species and perennial grass/shrub densities were not consistent with objectives and were =3 plants/m2. The average density for perennial grasses and shrubs was 2.10 plants/m2 with only 0.75 plants/m2 coming from seeded species. The average percent cover of perennial species in the third year was 6.79 % with 5.36 % coming from seeded species. There was no one species which composed the majority of the measurements.
   The data are inconsistent. This inconsistency is mainly due to the difference in aspect of the study plots. Plot 1 shows decreasing cover and density estimates as cheatgrass takes over the area from the few seedlings that initiated establishment. Plot 2 shows a more familiar time trend of decreasing density with increasing cover. This trend would be expected from a community establishing itself as plants initially compete for space with other immerging plants. Cheatgrass was present in the location of plot 2, but it did not dominate the area as in plot 1.
   If possible, longer than the three year rest period should be negotiated with the permittees, as that will help deminish the domination of the site by invasive annuals; in addition to giving the natural seeded grasses more time to mature.

Objectives: 1. Vegetative cover on this site was primarily Wyoming big sagebrush with little or no understory. Fire impacts have resulted in complete denuding of the landscape. Aerial seeding of 576 acres inaccessible to the seed drill is proposed. Species selected in the seed mix are intended to be fast rooting for stabilization and to limit the establishment and spread of new fire starts in an attempt to break the frequent fire cycle impacting the rest of the burned area while maintaining species diversity found on site pre-fire. Vegetative cover needs to be re-established to provide soil stability and to limit gully formation and sedimentation impacting access roads to private residences and prevent undue erosion from the site.\r\n2. Previous drill seeding treatments conducted adjacent to the proposed treatment area in 2007 were observed to be successful. Completion of the proposed action should maintain access to the private residence and limit impacts to Columbia Hill road. Since the site potential is very good and previous seeding actions were successful, the probability of success is high.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results: After driving all accessible roads within the burned area and stopping frequently to check ground conditions, it appeared that on the west side of the burned area thistles and cheatgrass invasion will be a problem in the future. Native bunchgrasses and previously seeded species were found in higher than anticipated quantity, but no new sagebrush regeneration was observed. Unseeded portions of the eastern side of the fire exhibited numerous forbs and thistles and fewer actively growing grasses. Areas seeded with the ES mix appeared to be growing in a \u201cdoghair\u201d manner, which may indicate that seeding in this area was successful. This new growth was especially evident in water collection points, which may indicate that broadcast seed was transported by surface water to the areas especially in need of stabilization.

Seed mixture would include Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush, forage kochia and Western yarrow. Actual_Implementation:
On January 23,2002 the Sheep Fire Wildlife Aerial Seeding Crucial Deer Winter Range began. The seeding was done via rental agreement with EI Aero. EI Aero supplied a helicopter and pilot, two seed buckets, fuel truck with crew and a seed mixer. The BLM supplied the ground crew ( five people) and one project inspector. The seed mixture for a 450 lb. bucket load was approximately 1151bs. Wyoming Big Sagebrush, 1251bs. Basin Big Sagebrush, 221bs. Western Yarrow and 190 lbs. Forage Kochia. This recipe was used to allow for the amount of Wyoming Big Sage available at the time. The ground was bare with from 20 to 50% snow cover (see photos). Seeding began in the northeast corner of the fire (T34N R48E sec16) and worked
southwest. Seeding finished that evening at around the Battle Creek area (T33N R46E sec26). A total of 6,045 lbs. of seed were used covering 1,650 acres today yielding 3.66 lbs./acre. I observed an even flow of seed from the bucket and a good even seed distribution in the snow on the ground.
On January 24, seeding resumed with the same crews. However, now the seed was sprayed with fertilizer in the mixer by a representative from Germ-N-8 who arrived from Washington. Ken Wilkenson and Tom Warren agreed to alter the seed mix to spread the remaining Wyoming Big Sage over the remainder of the project. Test results had not yet returned on more Wyoming Big Sage. The new ratio was approximately 160 lbs. Basin Big Sage and 80 lbs. Wyoming Big Sage along with 221bs. Western Yarrow and 190 lbs. Forage Kochia. The helicopter worked around the southern tip of the range and on toward the northwest, finishing around T33N R45E sec 2. By the end of the day the Wyoming Big Sage ran out as well as the Western Yarrow. A total of 8,370 lbs. of seed were used covering 2,366 acres today yielding 3.54Ibs./acre. Again I observed an even flow of seed from the bucket and a good even seed distribution in the snow on the ground.
On January 25, seeding resumed with the same crews. Fertilizer was again applied to the seed mix. The seed mix was now approximately 240 lbs. Basin Big Sage, 221bs. Western Yarrow (though this was not included in the first two buckets as I brought it from Elko in the morning) and 190 lbs. Forage Kochia. The Wildlife Aerial Seeding was finished by 0915 today. A total of 1,860 lbs. of seed were used today covering 683 acres yielding 2.7 lbs./acre. I observed an even flow of seed from the bucket. The totals for the project were 16,275 lbs. of seed over 4,699 acres averaging 3.46Ibs./acre.

Objectives: The purpose of the seeding is to provide forage and cover for wildlife, particularly, for sage grouse nesting and summer/brood rearing habitat, and winter range for mule deer and pronghorn antelope. Seeding this area would reduce the potential for the invasion of non-native invasive weed species.
Planned_Implementation: Sage Grouse Habitat Emphasis - Northern Portion of Burn Area: Every third swath within 9,402 acres, which equals 3,134 acres, would be seeded within selected public land sections primarily on the north portion of the burn area. Seed mixture would include Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush and Western yarrow. When possible, seed would be broadcast on snow to aid in germination and reduce seed consumption by rodents and birds.
Actual_Implementation:
On February 14, 2002 the Sheep Fire Wildlife Aerial Seeding, Sage Grouse Habitat Emphasis, North Side began. The seeding was done via rental agreement with EI Aero. EI Aero supplied a helicopter and pilot, seed buckets, fuel truck with crew and seed mixer. BLM supplied the ground crew ( six people) and one project inspector. The seed was sprayed with fertilizer in the
mixer by a representative from Germ-N-8. The recipe called for: 5,350 lbs. of Wyoming Big Sagebrush, 1,250 lbs. Basin Big Sagebrush, 350 lbs. Small Burnet, 450 lbs. Upland Alfalfa and 500 lbs. Western Yarrow over every third swath at a rate of 2.5 bulk lbs./acre. Seeding began at 11:48 and finished at approximately 1700. The day's totals were 4,275 lbs. of seed over 1,734
acres averaging 2.5 lbs./acre as called for. Due to the terrain and distance from the staging area on the northwest comer of the fire, I was unable to observe the seeding from an ATV.
On February 15, seeding resumed with the same crews. After working the northwest comer with the Interior Sage Grouse Habitat mix the staging area was moved to the top of Battle Creek (see photos). I was able to observe seeding from the ATV. Winds were approximately 10 to 15 mph. from the northeast on the ridges but lighter winds to calm in the lower areas. There were patches of snow in the drainages and on east facing slopes (see photos). Soils were damp due to snow melt and muddy in many drainages. There were a number of unburned islands throughout the area. I observed a steady even flow of seed from the bucket and the seed was not drifting much from the wind. It was difficult to observe the seed in the snow due to the amount of dirt and debris already on the snow and the rough surface due to wind and melting. The North Side mix areas of the seeding were completed by 14:55 with a total of 7,975 lbs. of seed over 3,050 acres averaging 2.6 lbs./acre. This was slightly above the rate called for but may be due to the number of unburned islands in the area (see photos).

Objectives: The fire killed the shrub component within the burn perimeter. It is anticipated that the grass and forb species in these treatment areas will re-sprout or reseed naturally.  The goal of reseeding the treatment areas with shrub species will help provide cover and forage for wildlife; reduce water erosion hazards by stabilizing soils; increase the rate at which native riparian vegetation is restored; maintain a healthy, productive, and diverse plant community; and minimize the establishment of exotic annual plants.  Cumulative losses of sagebrush communities continue to impact sage grouse populations across the Great Basin.  Conversion of sagebrush stands to grasslands due to wildland fire has been a continuing trend over the last decade.  Coupled with the sagebrush die off from caused from the Aroga Moth, the rehabilitation of sagebrush communities has become a high priority on the Elko District.  Sagebrush stands must be established within the burned area to act as future seed sources to allow the stands to repopulate hundreds of square miles.  Emphasis of these rehabilitation seedings have been placed on sage grouse.  Application of sagebrush seed will target areas that had the existing vegetation community that is being seeded.  This will ensure that seeded species are being applied in areas that are suitable for establishment and will increase the successfulness of the seeding. Wyoming and Basin sagebrush and Western Yarrow were seeded to provide cover for Sage Grouse.\r\n\r\nThe primary goal is to provide cover and forage for sage grouse.  Target areas formerly supporting sagebrush, ensuring seeded species are broadcast on areas suitable for establishment, to increase the seeding success. Establish one seeded plant per square meter, rooted firmly in soil, with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seeding establishment.  Stabilize soils to reduce erosion.  Increase restoration rate for native riparian vegetation.  Maintain a healthy, productive, and diverse plant community.  Minimize establishment of exotic annual plants.  Establish sagebrush stands within the burn for future seed sources.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerially seed approximately 4,006 acres of watershed drainages and known Wyoming Big Sagebrush sites with a mix of Western Yarrow, Wyoming Big Sagebrush, and Basin Big Sagebrush. 


Aerial seeding will be accomplished using a helicopter and seed bucket or broadcaster.  The aerial seed will be applied when weather conditions are favorable to allow for coverage by snow or adequate moisture, and thus will be applied in late fall or early winter.
Actual_Implementation: This treatment was implemented during January via helicopter through a contract agreement.  AgNav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  A project inspector ensured seeding was applied over the target area during desirable weather conditions to ensure seed is evenly distributed.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Sage grouse Aerial Wildlife Seeding was monitored at four locations, SPSG – 01, SPSG – 02, SPSG – 03 and SPSL – 01. 
Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Success was variable from monitoring location to monitoring location but germination rates were generally low.  At SPSG – 01, Western Yarrow was recorded at low density, Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  At SPSG – 02 no seeded species were recorded.  At SPSG – 03 all seeded species were recorded at very low densities.  At SPSL – 01, Western Yarrow was recorded at very low density.  Reconnaissance conducted crossing widely separated seedings of this treatment suggests some germination occurred across the treatment, but sampling suggests rates of germination and establishment were low.  Reconnaissance suggests Basin Big Sagebrush was more successful than Wyoming Big Sagebrush; densities recorded appear to confirm this. 
2008 – Seeded species appear to be increasing slowly at all three monitoring locations.  Success was lowest at SPSG – 02, where one Wyoming Big Sagebrush seedling was recorded, up from no seeded species recorded the first year.  At SPSG – 01 Western Yarrow density approached one-half plant per square meter.  SPSG – 03 Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density, Wyoming Big Sagebrush at low density, and Western Yarrow at a moderate density near one-quarter plant per square meter for a total seeded species density near one-half plant per square meter. 
2009 – At SPSG – 01 total seeded species density was moderate, exceeding one-third plant per square meter.  Western Yarrow made the greatest contribution; Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at low density.  At SPSG – 02 total seeded species density was very low, with only a few pants of Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush recorded.  At SGSP – 03 only Western Yarrow was recorded, at a low-to-moderate density.  At SPSL – 01 total seeded species density was low, with Western Yarrow making the greatest contribution, and only a few plants of Basin Big Sagebrush recorded.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was not recorded at any monitoring location during the final year.  This should be evaluated cautiously because Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at SPSG – 03 during 2007, and at SPSG – 01, – 02, and – 03 during 2008.   Overall, Western Yarrow was the most successful species seeded, recorded at all monitoring locations during the final year, and appearing to be well established at low densities.  Basin Big Sagebrush was more successful than Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush appears to be difficult to establish.  The Sheep Aerial Wildlife (low elevation) Seeding was partially successful.

Monitoring Results:  
2007 – Very little success was observed for the mule deer seedings.  Extensive reconnaissance was conducted across the mule deer seeding to locate sagebrush and Kochia germination. Accessibility problems discouraged sampling or reconnaissance in the southwest portion of the burn east of Rock Creek Canyon.  The monitoring plot (SPMD – 01) sampled an area with better success than other scattered areas of the mule deer treatment, so data collected there may present a more optimistic picture of germination success than is warranted for the treatment as a whole.  No Wyoming Big Sagebrush seedlings were recorded or observed.  Forage Kochia was recorded at low density, and observed off-transect. The Sheep Aerial Kochia Stabilization Seeding was monitored at one location (SPKO – 02) with a paced density transect. 
Monitoring Results:  
2007 – Greater success where (Kochia was seeded onto a drill seeding) may be the result surface disturbance resulting in a better seedbed.  Native release appeared good but the main contributor was low-growing Sandberg’s Bluegrass that survived the fire.  AT SPKO – 02, Kochia was unsuccessful after the first year.  One Kochia seedling was observed off-transect, none were recorded.  SPKO – 02 samples the aerial Kochia seeding where it was applied over an old Crested Wheatgrass seeding.  Low densities of establishing Kochia observed here may be attributed to drouthy conditions and to competition from well-established Crested Wheatgrass. 
2008 – No Forage Kochia was recorded. 
2009 – Forage Kochia was not recorded at SPKO – 02.  Forage Kochia seedlings were observed at very low density off transect, but appeared to have declined consistently during the monitoring period.  We may consider the Sheep Aerial (Kochia) Stabilization Seeding to be partially successful, but only marginally so.  The seeded area is relatively small, and ocular reconnaissance supports the extremely low density numbers for Forage Kochia recorded at the monitoring location.  The marginal success at SPKO – 02 is problematic.  The entire area near Rock Creek Ranch seems to have endured drouthy conditions from 2006 through early 2009, and apparently did not benefit from the abundant rainfall in late spring of 2009.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Currently, in the semiarid lands of the western states, we are experiencing a widespread increase
in the number of acres that are being converted from its native state (ie. Salt Desert shrub) to
Cheat grass. This conversion displaces more productive and diverse native vegetation. Cheat
grass (Bromus tectorum) is an annual brome grass that was introduced to the western states
toward the end of the settlement of the west. This exotic annual grass comes from the Russian
Steppe area. It provides the fine fuels base that allows wildland fires to carry through this shrub
type, which in its pre-settlement state would not have carried fire. The associated pattern of ever
more frequent wildfires has also had a heavy impact on the size of these fires because they spread
into adjacent vegetation types making suppression efforts much more difficult. As a result, fire
suppression costs in the Desert shrub areas has increased greatly. In an effort to significantly
reduce these costs, the Salt Lake Field Office is initiating an aggressive Fuel Break/Green
Stripping and vegetation treatment project. This would involve establishing a grid of less
flammable vegetation strips 300&$ wide throughout these areas to break up the fuels which will
reduce the size and complexity of these fires. As a result, the annual costs associated with fire
suppression will be reduced. The area designated in this proposed action is part of this project.

Objectives: The fire removed existing shrubs that were dominant on the site which served as general habitat for sage-grouse as well as sharp-tail grouse. The area is also mule deer winter range, which contains one of the highest winter populations of mule deer in SE Idaho. Previous fires that have affected the surrounding areas (which were not seeded or planted with sagebrush), continue to lack sagebrush cover. The area that burned had sagebrush at sufficient levels to be considered good S.G. habitat. The loss of this habitat further reduces the overall quality and quantity of the identified general S.G. habitat within the area.
Planned_Implementation: This will be a cooperative treatment with IDFG to aerial seed 1200 acres with sagebrush within designated sage grouse habitat that burned as a result of the fire. Seeding sagebrush will reducing the recovery time for the shrubs, which will in turn stabilize the loss of suitable S.G. habitat. Idaho Fish and Game have pledged to contribute money to be used toward application and or seed costs associated with this treatment. Distribution of seed will occur using aircraft to apply seed over uneven terrain. Criteria for the selection of treatment areas will include: deeper soil types, upper portions of ridgelines to allow for future seed dispersal, site were prevailing winds could help future seed dispersal. Seeding will occur in the late fall or early winter with snow on the ground to take advantage of winter and spring moisture.
Actual_Implementation: The Idaho Fish and Game Department contributed $10,000 to this project allowing the project area to increase from 1,200 acres to 3,012 acres. A solicitation for the aerial application for sagebrush seed was let on 2/3/2014. On March 12, 2014, Thomas Helicopters seeded 3,012 acres with Mountain Big Sagebrush seed at a rate of 0.5 lbs. /acre. 10 monitoring sites were established at the time of the seeding.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In March 2014, 10 monitoring plots were established as seed was applied to the hillside. Prior to the application of the seed, 1 meter hoops with white fabric were placed throughout the application area. Following the application of seed the hoops were visually checked for the presence of sagebrush seed. If seed was evident, a plot was established. In August of 2014, all 10 monitoring sites were sampled using a 100ft by 6ft belt transect. According to the monitoring the treatment produced 15 sagebrush seedlings per acre, this is below the objective of 225 sagebrush seedlings per acre therefore the objective has not been achieved to date. Even though few seedlings were encountered within the plots during the 2014 monitoring season, it was noted that seedling were present within the plot vicinity.

In July of 2015 all 10 monitoring sites established in 2014 were
resampled. An additional 7 plots were installed in 2015.

In 2015, all ten monitoring sites were revisited. An additional, four plots were installed within
the treatment area and three plots were installed outside of the treatment area (No Treatment).
The treatment area had an average of 16 sagebrush shrubs per acre while no sagebrush seedlings
were recorded within the No Treatment area. Though there was a slight increase in the number
of seedlings recoded within the treatment area, it is still below the objective of 225 seedlings per
acre.
In 2016, the original 10 plots were resampled. Only one plot had any recorded sagebrush
seedlings. When all transects were averaged together, a total of 22 seedings per acre was
calculated. This is well below the objective of 225 seedlings per acre. However, six new control
plots were established in 2016 in areas where no sagebrush seed was aerially applied. No
sagebrush seedlings were recorded at any of the control sites. Despite the fact that the treatment
failed to meet the set objective it is evident from the control plots (nine in total between 2015 and
2016) that the application of sagebrush seed did increase the number of sagebrush seedlings
within the area which will become mother plants to future sagebrush establishment.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
1) The ID team assessment of the fire determined that the potential for erosion and/or increased water flows out of the burned drainages (watersheds) were of concern. There are several large drainages that potentially could carry water and sediment onto existing roads. Several reservoirs could be dug deeper to catch potential increased runoff and sediment
reducing the potential damage to the road system. The existing road may need culverts cleaned and additional water bars/dips installed to handle the increased runoff. An Isolated heavy rain event occurred following the fire in September that caused ash and sediment to flow out of a burned side drainage emptying into North Drainage (a main road access to the
area) filling a livestock watering reservoir with sediment and overflowing it causing debris to deposit on the road way. It is expected that additional drainages will flow sediment onto roads as snow melts in the spring.

2) The fire occurred within mule deer winter range and Sage Grouse general habitat. There was high consumption of sagebrush within the burn area. This plan requests money to reestablish sagebrush through aerial seeding and possibly seedling planting in the future.

3) A high traffic trail & road system occurs within the burned area. The Samaria mountains draws recreationists from Utah and Idaho for wood cutting, hunting and other outdoor recreation. Due to its high use and current lack of vegetation, the potential for new pioneered trails along ridgelines and drainage bottoms is a high concern. Road closures are
needed to control cross country use through the burned area until vegetation has a chance to re-establish. The main road system will be closed until next year, at which time the main road may be opened. Following the opening of the main road this plan requests steel jack fencing to be installed in strategic places to close side trails and keep recreationists on open routes.

4) New infestations and expansion of existing weed populations is a high concern within the burn area. New infestations are expected to occur within the burn near existing trails and within the burn from seeds blown in from adjacent weed infestations. Monitoring and treatment of new infestations has been made part of this plan.

5) Approximately 800 acres of BLM designated commercial timber stands were severely burned within the fire perimeter. Approximately 300 ac are proposed for replanting (where it is expected that natural regeneration will not occur due to the burn severity) to help stabilize the soil, and provide important cover for deer and elk. This will require approximately
60,000 seedlings to plant 200 trees/acres.

6) The majority of the Samaria Grazing allotment was burned. There are several stock water pipelines and pasture fence lines that were burned by the fire. These improvements are critical for livestock grazing management within the allotment.

Planned_Implementation:
Aerially seed approximately 700 acres with Wyoming big sagebrush, Basin big sagebrush, Mountain big sagebrush and Western Yarrow in three treatment areas with mixes that are appropriate for the Ecological sites.  

•	Low Elevation Seeding - This seeding will consist of Wyoming big sagebrush and Western yarrow and will be aerially applied over approximately 435 acres of Wyoming sagebrush sites that are located below 5,500 feet through the bottomlands of the burned area.  This area is occupied by sage grouse, mule deer, and pronghorn antelope, which are all Resource Management Plan-featured species.  The Low Elevation Seed Mix will be aerially seeded with an every other swath pattern comprising of 870 acres.   
   
•	Mid Elevation Bottom Mix – This will be an aerial seeding of Basin big sagebrush over 145 acres shadowing watershed drainages where basin big sagebrush existed before the fire.  Treatment acres were identified by incorporating GIS data, soil maps, and ecological site descriptions, as well emphasizing areas around known sage grouse nesting areas.

•	Hi Elevation Mix – This will be an aerial seeding of mountain big sagebrush over approximately 120 acres where this type of sagebrush had existed before the fire. The Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding was monitored at four separate locations.  One location along a tributary of Little Rock Creek (WNWC – 03) was specifically established to monitor this treatment.  The other locations (WNWC – 02, WNWP – 01, WNWP – 02) were established to monitor aerial watershed protection seedings but are overlapped by the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding. 
Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush were “double-seeded” at WNWC – 02 where the Aerial Watershed Protection (Lahontan Cutthroat Trout) Seeding overlapped the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding, and at WNWP – 01 and WNWP – 03 where the Aerial Watershed Protection (Milligan/Chimney Creeks) Seeding overlapped the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding.  At locations where double-seeding occurred, seedlings contributed by either treatment cannot be separated: it is impossible to make a precise determination concerning which treatment was successful.  Since no rational separation of seedlings contributed by either treatment at the double-seeded locations can be made, total densities of the double seeded species are presented in the summaries for both treatments.  Caution should be applied when interpreting these density numbers with regard to either treatment: ultimately, we cannot know which treatment contributed any given seedling. 
2008 – Results varied at the five monitoring locations.  Total seeded species were recorded at low moderate density at WNWC – 02, at moderate density at WNWC – 03, and at very low density at WNWP – 03. Seeded species were not recorded at WNWP – 01 and WNWP – 02. 
2009 – Results continued to vary at the five monitoring locations, and fluctuated both up and down from 2008.  Generally, Western Yarrow appeared to be well-established at low density by the final year of the monitoring period.  At WNWC – 03, total seeded species exceeded the target density of one seeded plant per square meter, with Western Yarrow making the greatest contribution at nearly one plant per square meter.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was less successful.  The seeding was only fully successful at WNWC – 03.  At most sites the seeding was partially successful.  At WNWP – 01 no seeded species were observed during the monitoring period.  Ocular reconnaissance across widely separated seeded areas supports confidence in a conclusion of partially successful.  Generally, Basin Big Sagebrush was less successful than Western Yarrow.  Causes of the general lack of success of Basin Big Sagebrush in this seeding are unknown, because it usually establishes readily.

Density: The Aerial Guard Corral Mountain seed mix was aerially applied via fixed wing aircraft
to the public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was
comprised of Basin Big Sagebrush, Wyoming Sagebrush, and Sandberg’s bluegrass. In the AIM
plots that fell within this seeding treatment (Plots 13 and 14) the sagebrush establishment has
fully met success with a recorded average of 1.17 seeded sagebrush plants per meter. Grass
seedlings have not been successful at establishing in these sites: no seeded grasses were found in
2017 or 2018 monitoring. Objectives of the treatment are considered met when one big
sagebrush seedling and one and a half grass seedlings per square meter are established.
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was 80.3% in the treatment area. Perennial grasses have the
highest cover and dominate the plot with 50.0% cover. Sandburg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda) and
bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoregnaria spicata) have the highest cover of perennial grasses,
however, native, deep rooted Basin wildrye (Leymus cinerus), squirreltail (Elymus elymoidies),
and rhizomatous thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus) were also associated species on the
plots. Despite the native regrowth of perennial grasses, cheatgrass does have a 32.3% cover.
Annual forb cover, however, comes from a majority of native species like 20.7% tall annual
willow herb (Epilobium brachycarpum) cover.
Gaps: Gaps in canopy foliar cover have decreased in occurrence from 2017 monitoring, creating
a positive effect. Gaps in canopy cover that were the size and frequency observed in the seeding
treatment are generally shorter than 100 cm. Canopy cover should be preventing wind and water
erosion from occurring on the plot, however due to site specific silty and sandy soils, erosion was
frequently encountered in the treatment area.

2018: An average of approximately twenty-nine (28.5) different plant species was observed

within the 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plots.

Objectives: For purpose of biotic integrity, establish desirable species on 629 acres at an average of 3 perennial plants per square meter within\r\n3 years. For purpose of soil and site stability establish desirable species at 20-40 percent cover seeded across the seeded area within 2 years.
Planned_Implementation: Reseeding the Burn Area and Temporally Closing it to Cattle Use:\r\nThe Phoenix Fire will be reseeded with three different methods. Approximately 6,063 acres fall within the flats and can be treated via ground seeding with a mix of drill, and broadcast (with and without chain harrow incorporation). Then in the higher steeper slopes (approximately 629 acres) seeds will be applied aerially. While all seeds are subject to availability, the drill seed mix will primarily consist of grasses: Agropyron fragile (Siberian Wheatgrass), Leymus cinereus (Great Basin Wildrye), Distichlis spicata (Inland Saltgrass), Elymus wawawaiensis (Snakeriver Wheatgrass), Elymus elymoides (Bottlebrush Squirreltail), Achnatherum hymenoides (Indian Ricegrass). There will also be one forb: Sphaeralcea munroana (Munroe's Globemallow), and one shrub/subshrub: Atriplex confertifolia (Shadscale). Six different grasses will be applied aerially on the fire. These grasses are Agropyron fragile (Siberian Wheatgrass), Leymus cinereus (Great Basin Wildrye), Elymus elymoides (Bottlebrush Squirreltail), Achnatherum hymenoides (Indian Ricegrass), Pseudoroegneria spicata ssp. spicata (Bluebunch Wheatgrass) and Festuca idahoensis (Idaho Fescue). The ground seeding equipment will avoid rock outcrops, unburned islands, and any identified historical properties. Seeding will occur in the fall, winter, and early spring, shortly before anticipated winter snowfall to assist with propagation.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial seeding happened in December\r\n\r\nFY2020 - All plots were revisited in 2020.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2018:
Discussion: Battle Mountain District personnel utilized Jornada’s Shiny tool to randomly create six monitoring sites within the fire, two of these plots were within the aerial seeding area, 3 in the drill seeding area and one was in a area that was not seeded (See Table 1 for plot information). Each monitoring site was within a different soil Map Unit from the United States Department of Agriculture’s Web Soil Survey and all of the soil types found within the fire were looked at. The results of these monitoring sites that were visited are shown in Table 2 and 3. Monitoring data recorded included vegetation density and cover using photo points, quadrat density counts, line-point intercept, canopy gap, and perennial basal gap monitoring methods as described in: Monitoring Manual for Grassland, Shrubland and Savanna Ecosystems, Volume 1: Quick Start, Herrick et al, 2005, p36. Paced density quadrat count methods (developed by Elko BLM staff and advised by Rangeland Monitoring in Western Uplands, George Ruyle et al., University of Arizona, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, 2006, p 16) were also used to establish number and type of plants per meter squared. At the time of plot establishment, no seeding had happened on the fire. Seeding didn’t happen because the site was sprayed for cheatgrass in April of 2018 and the rest of the FY was a rest year to allow the chemical to have an impact on the fire, and to allow the chemical residual to degrade enough not to effect the seeded species, and then waiting for the ideal time of year for seed to be placed on/in the ground.
Results: See Tables below for a summary of data found. Since this was the first year of monitoring there is no data to compare the trends with, but this fire has not reached objectives yet.
Recommendations: Continue monitoring.
FY 2019:
Discussion: Fire was aerial seeded in November 2018 and drill seeded November 2018 to January 2019. All the plots were revisited in 2019.
Results: This fire is trending towards less annuals and more perennials, as well as better species richness. See tables below for a summary of data found.
Recommendation: Continue closure but discuss with range about opening it next summer. Continue monitoring.
FY 2020:
Discussion: All plots were revisited in 2020.
Results: The drilled portion of the fire has reached the objective but the aerial seeding portion of the fire has not. See tables below for a summary of data found and areas monitored.
Recommendation: Continue to monitor the fire and continue to allow grazing in the flats.
FY 2021:
Discussion: Two plots representative of overall burned area and treatment units were revisited.
Results: In the higher elevations of the burned area, perennial grass and shrub cover increased while perennial forbs remained the same. Annual invasive grass cover decreased, likely due to drought conditions and lack of precipitation, which allowed for the increased cover of annual invasive forbs. In the lower elevation, there were no annual invasive grasses or forbs present due to lack of precipitation. However, perennial grass cover increased significantly. Presence of both native and non-native seeded species indicates successful seeding establishment within the area in 2020. The higher elevation and lower elevation areas have met cover and density objectives.
Recommendations: Continue to monitor to see if these rates are confirmed again next year, especially if more precipitation is received this year.
FY 2022:
Discussion: Two plots representative of overall burned area and treatment units were revisited.
Results: Perennial grass and shrub cover decreased slightly within the plots monitored in FY22. However, overall density of perennial grasses increased significantly from FY20. Density objectives are currently being met within the aerial seeding and drill seeding treatment areas.
Recommendations: Continue to monitor through renewables program.

Treatment was an aerial herbicide application of Imazapic in the fall of 2016, followed by an
aerial seeding in the winter of 2016-2017 and a drill seeding the following winter of 2017-2018.
The aerial seeding mix was applied via aircraft to the public burned land in areas selected to be
in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Wyoming Big
Sagebrush, Western Yarrow, and Blue Flax. AIM Plots 04 and 05 were monitored in 2019. The
sagebrush establishment is showing some success: there was one seeded sagebrush recorded at

season.
Forb seedlings were not recorded in 2019 surveys when they were over half way towards full
establishment success in these sites in 2018: 0.80 seeded blue flax plants per square meter were
recorded in the second growing season. However, due to the fact that there were no blue flax
plants to be found in the first growing season (after the aerial seeding), the established blue flax

seedling and one and a half forb species (yarrow or flax) seedlings per square meter are
established.
The trend results here indicate that aerially seeding forbs and shrubs in the winter/spring
immediately following the fall aerial application of Imazapic (herbicide for annual grass control)

However, regrowth of Sandberg bluegrass and crested wheatgrass was observed on the plots.

grasses have 39.7% cover. Cheatgrass cover had reduced cover (12.5%) in 2017, an intended
positive correlation to the aerial herbicide treatment. Cheatgrass cover more-than doubled, to
33.3% at the two plots, from the first to third growing seasons. However, this cover of cheatgrass
is less cover than all other non-imazapic treated areas in the Hot Pot rehab area. Native perennial
plant regrowth includes 29.7% perennial grass cover and 1.3% perennial forb cover. Sandberg’s

Planned_Implementation:
Aerial seed approximately 2,725 acres with an
every other swath coverage in low elevation areas with a mixture of forage kochia, Sandbergs
bluegrass, and Western yarrow. This area is located outside GSG habitat, but within crucial
mule deer winter range. The seeding will provide mule deer with a forage base during the

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Density: The Aerial Horseshoe Mountain Treatment seed mix was applied aerially via aircraft to
the public burned land in accordance with the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised
of Wyoming Sagebrush, Sandberg’s Bluegrass, and Blue Flax. In the AIM plots that fell within
this seeding treatment (Plots 42, 44, 45, and 46) the sagebrush establishment has nearly met
success: there are a recorded average of 0.95 seeded sagebrush plants per meter. Blue flax
seedlings have been showing progress towards establishment success in these sites: 0.19 seeded
blue flax plants per square meter were recorded in 2018 monitoring. Objectives of the treatment
are considered met when one big sagebrush seedling and one and a half forb species (yarrow or
flax) seedlings per square meter are established.
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was 80.5% in the Aerial Horseshoe Mountain Treatment
area. Perennial grasses have 25.5% cover, including 20.3% Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda)
and 4.5% basin wildrye (Leymus cinerus). Cheatgrass has 50.8% cover while annual forbs have
14.4% cover and native perennial forbs have 15.9% cover. Overall, the site’s native perennial
plant species are still competing well against the annual invasive grasses and forbs.
Gaps: Gaps in canopy foliar cover have decreased significantly in occurrence and length from
2017 monitoring, creating a positive effect for controlling erosion on the sites. However, an
average of 2.57 meters of the 25 meter transects are comprised of gaps larger than 200 cm. Gaps
of this size are detrimental to the site in that they allow wind and water erosion to occur. Canopy
gaps greater than 25 cm represent only 25% of the average 25 m transect, therefore canopy cover
is generally preventing wind and water erosion from occurring on the plot.

Objectives: The objective is to prevent sagebrush communities to transitioning into an annual plant state\r\nand restoring essential forage and cover for greater sage grouse.
Planned_Implementation:
The BLM proposes to aerial seed a total of 124 acres of public land managed by BLM
that was burned by the Paradise Fire. Seeding would occur in the fall or winter with a
preference for application in late fall or early winter. The possible species the project
would seed with are bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata spp.spicata),
fourwing saltbush (Atriplex canescens), hoary tansyaster (Machaeranthera canescens),
rocky mountain beeplant (Cleome serrulata), scarlet globemallow (Sphaeralcea
coccinea), and Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis). All
species proposed for aerial seeding are native.
Actual_Implementation:
Project was implemented using a Call When Needed
helicopter and fire crew staff.
It is policy and a first choice to use native species for
restoring quality wildlife habitat within a Wilderness Study
Areas. The species that were seeded for this project are;
Wyoming sagebrush, rocky mountain beeplant, tansyaster,
fourwing saltbrush , bluebunch wheatgrass, and poa
secunda. Wyoming sagebrush and bluebunch wheatgrass are
listed as major plant species on the site by the rangeland
ecological site descriptions provided by NRCS.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results Summaries:
Rangeland Ecological Site: R025XY19NV Loamy 8-10 P.Z.: The reference plant community
is dominated by Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis, Achnatherum thurberianum, and
Pseudoroegneria spicata. Reference vegetation community composition is approximately 65%
grasses, 30% shrubs, and 5% forbs.
T69-A1Fairbanks-PAR-16
Treatment: Aerially seeded with Cleome serrulata, Machaeranthera canescens, Atriplex
canescens, Pseudoroegneria spicata, Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis, Poa
secunda
2017: This plot did not meet the objective for density of seeded species. This plot did
meet the ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. For a photograph of
line 1, see Figure 3
2016: This plot did not meet the objective for density of seeded species. This plot did not
meet the ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. The plot was
dominated by Bromus tectorum and Sisymbrium altissimum. Few deep-rooted, perennial
grasses were found on site. Some A. tridentata ssp. wyomingensis and Tetradymia
canescens survived the fire in rocky outcrops. The site is very gravelly and cobbly. P.
secunda was seeded and was fairly common, but was not counted due to the difficulty of
distinguishing individual stalks this late in the season. The crew noted that the P. secunda
was likely resprouting from plants that existed at the plot pre-burn and were not from the
seeding. Also, the four A. tridentata ssp. wyomingensis found at the plot were unburned
plants and were not seeded. For a photograph of line 1, see Figure 2
Conclusions:
The Paradise Fire did not meet any of the ESR or livestock objectives for recovery post
burn after the first year of monitoring. Non-native annuals dominate the fire area as well as the
surrounding area. There are areas of rock outcrops and unburned islands where native plants,
especially Wyoming sagebrush and bluebunch wheatgrass, have survived the fire and are
recruiting. No further seeding is planned at this time. Depending on funding the survey and
treatment of noxious weeds will continue to occur…

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Perennial frequency was calculated from density data and represents the frequency occurrence of
any perennial species per \xbc meter squared, 3 lines combined (150 samples). Perennial frequency
is easily on track to meet the targeted 35% relative frequency objective. Total perennial
frequency averaged approximately 86 % for two monitored sites. Perennial composition is
derived from frequency and represents the total percentage of seeded species, re-established
perennials, and annuals/exotics for each plot (150 samples). Composition of perennial species in
2018 averaged approximately 66% for two monitored sites.

The ESR drill seeding and chaining treatments on the Sage Fire show good results after the third year following the fire. Seedlings are getting successfully established and re-established perennials show good recovery across the burn, pointing toward the continued success of ESR treatments. The objective as to achieve a relative frequency of desirable perennial species of 35% within 3 years. The seeding treatment results are impressive, achieving a total perennial frequency averaged 70.91% for the monitoring sites in 2020. Desirable perennials are competing with cheatgrass and have limited its presence, as can be observed in comparing treated areas to neighboring sites.
Seeded perennial vegetation is aiding in holding the soil in place across the burned area. No noxious weed were observed during monitoring in June 2020 and weed treatments in July 2020. Squarrose knapweed that has been problematic in the area has been reduced due to the cooperative management between Tooele County and the BLM Salt Lake Field Office.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2017: Two sites were monitored using Nested Plot Frequency transects in the Rhyolite ESR on July 13,
2017. Road access into this ESR remains limited. ESR treatments on this fire finally met the
40% perennial composition objective for the first time in 2017, the fifth year following the fire.
The 40% composition objective is measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation.
Although the north monitoring site (CH1) continues to be dominated by cheatgrass, seeded and
re-established perennials are showing healthy vigor and increasing in frequency. The relative
frequency of seeded and re-established perennials at this site was up to approximately 44% in
2017, over 29% in 2016 and just 13% in 2015. Although, the monitoring site in Birch Canyon
has been severely invaded by cheatgrass, the relative frequency of perennial species at this site
was stable at approximately 54%. Relative frequency of perennial vegetation averaged
approximately 49% for both monitoring locations.

Objectives:
Objectives for aerial seeding with seed mixes containing grasses and shrubs are as follows:
1. Obtain an average of 1 seeded plant per square meter by the end of the fifth year following fire ignition, which occurred on 9/1/2017.
2. Obtain 50% or greater perennial cover of the low potential perennial plant cover for the appropriate ecological site by the end of the fifth year following fire containment.
3. The seeding would result in lower abundance (density and cover) of invasive annual plant species, and a higher abundance of desirable perennial plant species than the unseeded control areas.
4. Seeded species would be well established and reproducing.
Without treatment the burned areas are increasingly susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the 
Greater Sage-Grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter 
months. Seeding occurred on sites that do not have the likelihood of naturally recovering from the fire. Areas were seeded 
with perennial species to reduce the dominance of Bromus tectorum.

Planned_Implementation:
The BLM proposes to aerial seed a total of 13,275 acres of land managed by BLM that was
burned by the Tohakum 2 Fire. Seeding would occur in January or February 2018 in areas not
treated with Imazapic. In areas treated with Imazapic, seeding would occur between December
2018 and January 2019. Five seed mixes would be used.
Four mixes will be used in year one aerial seeding treatments, in January or February 2018:

A mountain big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana) seed mix would be applied to
8,500 acres at upper elevations in the Selenite and Lake Ranges. Proposed species for this mix
include mountain big sagebrush, Sandberg bluegrass, and bluebunch wheatgrass
(Pseudoroegneria spicata).
Actual_Implementation:
Aerially Seeding with three different seed mixes in areas with 
high shrub mortality. 
The mountain sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana) 
is mixed with Poa secunda and Psudoroegneria spicata.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
After the third year after treatments and only three plots monitored, monitoring results show that
one of the plots have met their plant density objectives. All failed the ESR perennial objective 
except one, that plot was passed the objective by .4 plants per meter2
. The contrast between 
these plots shows what a complicating fire this was and the confusing monitoring establishments.
Multiple plots needed to be discontinued due to the location of the 2018 established plot outside 
of the burn. More plots still needed to be removed from 2018 due to funding and treatment
changes. A conclusion is that the seeding failed along with an herbicide spray that removed all 
vegetation except Russian thistle (See Figure 10). Even the plot that made a successful recovery 
did it without a single seeded plant. The lower elevations plots had much more annual plants and 
the recovery will be difficult. There are no more treatments planned for the Tohakum 2 fire.

Objectives: Maintain a sufficient quality, and\r\ndiversity of habitat and forage for livestock, wildlife, and wild horses through natural\r\nregeneration and/or vegetation manipulation methods.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 9,125 acres would be aerial seeded. About 1,393 acres would be aerial seeded
to a low elevation seed mix then "one pass" chained to cover the seed and 7,732 acres would
be aerial seeded to a high elevation seed mix. All seed rates are PLS (Pure Live Seed), but the
seed is seldom provided by PLS: it is usually at a bulk rate, meaning, for example, that 2 1/2 or 3
pounds bulk rate may have to pass through the drill to actually put 2 pounds PLS on/in the soil.

Aerial seeding would be done in the winter to take advantage of fall/winter moisture,
including snow.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial Seeding (unit. Acres) 9,125/units: @ $45.28 /unit -Total $413,175.87.\r\n\r\nThe high elevation seeding took place on February 4 thru 15,2002
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2003 - virtually no seedling
establishment but good native response in 3 of 4 study areas aerially seeded only.

excellent
seedling establishment in aerially seeded and chained area; compilation of 2003 data
incomplete.

Four of 5 monitoring studies were established in the aerially seeded portion of project with the fifth
one placed in the aerially seeded and chained area. Livestock grazing occurred in 2 of 5 study areas.
There was virtually no seedling establishment, but native response was good in 3 of 4 ‘aerially
seeded only’ study areas. Seedling establishment was excellent in the ‘aerially seeded and
chained’ area.
Monitoring of both density and percent cover shows that emergence, particularly natives, was
high the first year. Percent cover of forbs, grasses and shrubs increased each year following,
while the number of all categories has slowly decreased. This decline in numbers is to be
expected as plants compete for resources during the early phases of revegetation. Since
cheatgrass did not seem to be invading the area, competition from cheatgrass is ruled out as a
factor in the decline.

Lessons Learned/What Worked & Didn’t Work:
The probability of seeding success increases when chaining is utilized after aerial seeding. In
areas where the understory is adequate to provide a seed bank that will regenerate the vegetation
complex, it may not be as imperative to chain or even seed. However, other monitoring studies
have shown that even with an adequate seed bank for revegetation, cheatgrass invasion is still a
threat.

Objectives:
The objective of the aerial seeding treatment is to revegetate the burned area with a
well-adapted array of species that will provide essential forage and cover for wildlife including
sage-grouse and will promote structural and species diversity within the burned area.
Objectives of the treatment will be to establish one native forb seedling per square meter in
post-fire monitoring within two growing seasons.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerial Seeding:
Approximately 822 acres would be seeded in the fall/winter of 2017/2018, with species appropriate for the site based on resistance, resilience, ecological site descriptions, provisional seed transfer zones and wildlife habitat concerns. Seed would be applied using an every other swath pattern (411 actual seeded acres).

Coal Aerial Mix: 
Aerial seed approximately 411 acres of PHMA and GHMA GSG habitat and pronghorn summer range habitat with Wyoming big sagebrush and western yarrow using an every other swath pattern.
Actual_Implementation: The seed mix was comprised of Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium v. occidentalis)\r\nand Wyoming Big Sagebrush (Artemesia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2019 Density Results:
Density: The seed mix was comprised of Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium v. occidentalis)
and Wyoming Big Sagebrush (Artemesia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis). The rehab objective of
1 firmly rooted forb per square meters has not been met. There were no seeded species observed
within the density frames or on the plot. Native perennial grasses, such as small-form Sandberg
bluegrass and thickspike wheatgrass and large-form bluebunch wheatgrass, Thurber’s
needlegrass, and squirreltail, are establishing themselves, however, with 18.58 perennial grasses
per square meter.
S3 Aerial Seeding
2019 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was high (85.3%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass
(Bromus tectorum) (46.7% cover). Perennial forbs contributed to 4.7% of the canopy cover while
perennial grasses contributed to 48.7% of the canopy cover. Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda)
and basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus) were the most common species among the perennial
grasses with 16.7% cover and 20.7% cover, respectively. While the plot is experiencing
significant perennial regrowth, the annual cover is also high and will need to take up less of the
ecological niche for seeded shrubs and forbs to establish themselves.
Gaps and Erosion: Coal AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland CLAYPAN 10-12 P.Z. ecosite
(R025XY018NV) in former Artemisia arbuscula / Pseudoroegneria spicata - Achnatherum
thurberianum ( / little sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass - Thurber's needlegrass) vegetation
communities. Canopy cover had frequent gaps between 51-100cm which took up 15% of the 25
meter transects. Gaps of 200cm plus were also common at 11% of the 25 meter transects. The
occurrence of these gaps could contribute to impaired soil and hydrologic function on the site.
Erosion was frequently observed in a few pedestals, an active gully, long and common water
flow patterns, and common deposition/runoff. This much erosion has caused a departure from
expected site stability and recovery of native perennial species will be important to re-establish
stability.
Species Richness: Twenty one (21) different plant species were observed within the 2,827.4
square meter monitoring plot.
2019 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives have not yet been met for these treatments. Seeded species
were not observed on the plot and the presence of invasive annuals was common. There was no
allotment closure issued for this area but it advised that the area receives appropriate rest so that
the rehab objectives can be met and annual species density is reduced. Stability in temperatures
and precipitation in 2020 could provide an additional good growing season with more water
availability and seedling success.

2020 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was high (76.7%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) (35.3% cover). Canopy cover had frequent gaps between 51-100cm which took up 7.1% of the 25 meter transects. Gaps of 21-50 cm plus were also common at 13.4% of the 25 meter transects. The occurrence of these gaps could contribute to impaired soil and hydrologic function on the site. Erosion was frequently observed in a few pedestals, an active gully, long and common water flow patterns, and common deposition/runoff. 2020 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives have not yet been met for these treatments. Seeded species were not observed on the plot and the presence of invasive annuals was common. There was no allotment closure issued for this area, but it advised that the area receives appropriate rest and grazing management so that the rehab objectives can be met, and annual species density is reduced. Stability in temperatures and precipitation in 2021 could provide an additional good growing season with more water availability and seedling success.


2022 MONITORING RESULTS
Density Results:
2020: The rehab objective of 1 firmly rooted seeded forb per square meters has not been met. There were no seeded species observed within the density frames or on the plot. Native perennial grasses, such as small-form Sandberg bluegrass and large-form bluebunch wheatgrass, Thurber’s needlegrass, and squirreltail, are establishing themselves, with 8.6 perennial grasses per square meter.
2022: The rehab objective of 1 firmly rooted seeded forb per square meters has still not been met. No seeded species were observed for the second year, native regrowth of grasses decreased from 2020 but regrowth of forbs and shrubs were present in good numbers, 3.33/m2 and 1.25/m2, respectively.
AIM Data Results:
Cover
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was high (76.7%) in part due to dominance of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) (35.3% cover). Perennial forbs contributed to 8.0% of the canopy cover while perennial grasses contributed to 52% of the canopy cover. Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) and basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus) were the most common species among the perennial grasses with 16% cover and 16% cover, respectively. While the plot is experiencing significant perennial regrowth, the annual cover is also high and will need to take up less of the ecological niche for seeded shrubs and forbs to establish themselves.
2022: Average foliar canopy cover decreased significantly from 2021, 76.7% down to 42.0%. The biggest decrease in foliar indicators was observed in perennial grasses, from 52% down to 6.3%, a decrease of 45.7% total. Annual grasses (cheatgrass) also saw a large decrease down to 7.8%, not taking over the space left behind by the decrease of perennial grasses yet and this will need continued monitoring and potential treatment to keep cheatgrass from dominating in the future.
Gaps and Erosion
2020: Canopy cover had frequent gaps between 51-100cm which took up 7.1% of the 25 meter transects. Gaps of 21-50 cm plus were also common at 13.4% of the 25 meter transects. The occurrence of these gaps could contribute to impaired soil and hydrologic function on the site. Erosion was frequently observed in a few pedestals, an active gully, long and common water flow patterns, and common deposition/runoff. This much erosion has caused a departure from expected site stability and recovery of native perennial species will be important to re-establish stability.
2022: Canopy cover increased largely in the 101-200cm range (32.4%) and the >200cm (14.1%) when compared to the 2020 observations. The increase in larger gaps could lead to further degradation of the plot and allow for cheatgrass to spread and dominate the site. No major signs of erosion were observed on the plot which could indicate progression towards rehabilitating the soils, allowing for perennials to reestablish with further management.
2022: Total number of species reduced by 21 since 2020. Each growth habit had at least two less species observed, the largest drop seen in perennial forbs. The distribution of species is very similar to 2019’s observations except for a loss of 6 annual forb species. The loss of 4 perennial grass species along with the increase of annual grass cover is of concern for the future success of the site.

Recommendations:
2022: The ESR rehabilitation objectives have not yet been met for these treatments. Seeded species were not observed on the plot and the presence of invasive annuals increased significantly since 2020. There was no allotment closure issued for this area and cattle disturbance was observed, so it advised that the area receives appropriate rest and grazing management so that the rehab objectives can be met, and annual species density is reduced.
