Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
*2019*
Density Results:
The seed mix was comprised of black sagebrush (Artemisia nova), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), and western yarrow (Achillea millefolium v. occidentalis). The rehabilitation objectives will be considered met for this seeding if 0.3 native shrubs, 1 native forb, and 3 native grasses per square meter are observed within three to five years. Only seeded grasses were observed within the density frames. Regrowth of Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), a small-form perennial grass, and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) and Thurber’s needlegrass (Achnatherum thurberianum) was evident on the plot.

AIM Data Results:
- Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was high (76%) in part due to the high cover (57.5%) of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum). Perennial grasses provided the second highest cover at 16.3%,
followed by perennial forbs at 9.2%, annual forbs at 4.9%, and shrubs at 4.3% cover. Though seeded species were seldom observed on the plots, recovery of perennials was evident. Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) had the second highest cover across the four plots (11.8%) and silvery lupine (Lupinus argenteus) had the third highest cover (7.2%).
- Erosion: Cottonwood AIM Plots 01 and 02C are located in a Rangeland South Slope 12-14” P.Z. ecosite (R025XY009NV) in a former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana – Purshia tridentata / Pseudoroegneria spicata ( / mountain big sagebrush – antelope bitterbrush / bluebunch wheatgrass) vegetation community. - Gaps: Gaps on the plot were mostly from 25 to 50 cm in length but only represented 8.4% of the average 25m transects. However, canopy cover is primarily composed of cheatgrass, which is not ideal for plant community composition and true cover potential for the sites.
- Species Richness: An average of thirty-two (31.8) different plant species were observed within the four 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plots.

active creek runs through this plot. Few pedestals and waterflow paths were observed on the plot. Overall wind and water erosion at the site was not apparent.

Cottonwood AIM Plot 04 is located in a Rangeland Loamy 8-10” P.Z. ecosite (R025XY019NV) ecosite in a former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis / Achnatherum thurberianum Achnatherum hymenoides ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber’s needlegrass – Indian ricegrass) vegetation community. 2022 ESR Monitoring report
S3 Aerial Seed Mix
Red Springs AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland Loamy 8-10” P.Z. ecosite (R025XY019NV) in a former Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis/ Achnatherum thurberianum – Achnatherum hymenoides ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber’s needlegrass – Indian ricegrass) vegetation community.
The seed mix was comprised of bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata spp. spicata), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium v. occidentalis), Blue flax (Linum perenne) and Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp vaseyana).

Density Results
2020: The rehab objective of 3 native grasses per square meter have been exceeded in quantity in AIM Plot 01. Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) was observed in the frames and some of those accounted for as seeded could also represent regrowth. Seeded forbs or shrubs were observed and observations of .08 forb and 0.41 shrubs are rehabilitation success indicators. Regrowth of Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), a small-form grass, and squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) was observed.
2022: The rehabilitation objective of 3 native grasses/m2 have been met when the native regrowth is taken into account but the density of seeded grasses alone falls short of the objective. This is a major decline from 2019 and 2020 when this objective was easily achieved. Sandberg bluegrass and squirreltail were still present along with Great Basin wildrye.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was moderate (50.7%) in part due to cover (16%) of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum). Annual forbs provided cover at 12% including clasping pepperweed (Lepidium perfoliatum), and desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum), Despite the high invasive grass cover the perennial, native bunchgrasses are showing recovery with a combined 15.3% cover. Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) attained 4.7% cover, basin wildrye (Leymus cinerus) had 5.3% cover and Squirreltail (Elymus elymoidies) had 4% cover. Native annual and perennial forbs were also showing recovery (18.6%).
2022: Average foliar cover was moderate at 68.7%, an increase of 18.0% since 2020. Annual forbs took over the dominance on the plot, increasing to 26.5% while perennial grasses and forbs decreased by 13.8% total. The majority of the annual forb cover is comprised of desert madwort (Alyssum desertorum), a highly invasive species in disturbed areas.

Gaps and Erosion
2020: Gaps on the plot were mostly at the 101-200cm range in length and represented 7.5% of the average 25m transects. Canopy cover represents 74% of the average 25m transects and this can be attributed largely to annual plant cover. These plants likely will not provide much soil stability for the site. Pedestalling was found to be common with common water flow patterns and common deposition/runoff was observed while the site’s overall slope was 10%. These factors are overall a moderate departure from expected conditions and therefore make wind and water erosion a concern for the site.
2022: Gaps on the plot increased significantly since 2020, most notably for gaps greater than 200cm, from 0.0% in 2020 to 58.8% in 2022. The only size range that decreased was 25-50cm from 9.0% to 4.9%. A gully 4ft wide by 2ft deep was noted on the southeast side of a hill just outside the plot and a large amount of long and interconnected waterflow patterns were observed. These signs of potential soil and site erosion in conjunction with the increased gaps observed could indicate overall degradation of the site health.

Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderately high at 24 individual species identified though this is a decrease of 4 total species from 2020. Perennial grasses and forbs do outnumber their annual counterparts but their coverage on the plot is dominated by the annual forbs observed.

Recommendations 2020: The ESR objectives have not been completely met for the site. However, regrowth of native grasses is evident. There was an allotment closure issued for Crane Springs allotment, Crane Springs pasture where Plot 01 is located. The allotment closure objective of three seeded species per square meter has been met but it is advised that additional rest be given to the area to allow for the establishment of seeded species.
2022: The ESR objectives have not been completely met for the site and regrowth of native grasses has decreased significantly. There was an allotment closure issued for Crane Springs allotment, Crane Springs pasture where Plot 01 is located. The allotment closure objective of three seeded species per square meter has been met but it is advised that continued rest be given to the area to allow for the establishment of seeded species.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The Red Springs fire will continue to have residual effects across the landscape for many years, but the planning, treatments, and monitoring accomplished in the last year have provided a steppingstone to continue with the restoration efforts throughout the burn area. One of the biggest lessons learned is that restoration takes time when you are dealing with environmental effects. There are many factors that go into restoring burn areas, some are human, but many are environmental. Goals and objectives will continue to be developed for restoring the Red Springs Fire and the lessons learned from this fire will be used for future planning in Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation.

Density Results
2020: The rehab objective of 1 native forb/m2, 0.3 native shrubs/m2, and 3 seeded species/m2 has not been met. No seeded species were observed but native regrowth of grasses was relatively robust.
2021: The rehab objective as stated above have not been met. Seeded shrub and density increased but not enough to meet the objective. Native regrowth of grasses however decreased since 2020 but native regrowth of shrubs was relatively robust.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives have not been met and have moved further away from meeting those objectives. No seeded shrubs were observed and seeded grasses decreased. Native regrowth of grasses increased very slightly but forbs and shrubs decreased significantly from 2021.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2020: Foliar canopy cover was very low at only 4.0% with all of the cover consisting of perennial grasses.
2021: Foliar canopy cover remained very low at 4.7% and perennial grasses remained most dominant but annual grasses, annual forbs, and shrubs were included for the first time.
2022: Foliar canopy cover increased significantly rising to 21.3%, however the large increase is almost entirely due to the increase in annual forbs (13.5%) across the plot. Perennial grasses were still present but the increase in annual forbs and annual grasses filling in the gaps is of concern for the health and rehabilitation ability of the plot.
Gaps and Erosion
2020: Canopy gap was highest in the >200cm range at 38.8% of a transect line. Given the extremely low foliar cover this amount of gap is relatively low.
2021: Ninety (90) percent of the transect lines are occupied by gaps in canopy cover, the majority of which is >200cm at 88.4% total. No rills or sheet erosion were observed, but an active gully, extensive pedestalling, water flow patterns, and deposition and runoff were observed.
2022: Canopy gap decreased and the distribution of gap across each size class was more spread out across the size classes leaving gaps >200cm lower than in 2021 (59.1%) but still the most dominant of the gap sizes. No evidence of soil erosion was observed on the plot, an improvement from 2021’s observations.
Species Richness
2021: Species richness was moderate with 20 individual species identified on the plot. This is an increase of 6 species since 2020 with annual forbs, perennial forbs, and shrubs increasing in their numbers of species observed.
2022: Species richness was moderate with 19 individual species identified on the plot. This is only a decrease of 1 species since 2021 but annual forbs increased by one species while shrubs decreased by 2 species.
Recommendations:
2020: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial and drill seedings have not been fully met, and some of the treatments have not been completed. Perennial grasses show signs of some establishment beginning on the plot. There was a grazing closure issued for the Shafter fire area. It is advised that the fire area is reviewed and receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish.
2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial and drill seedings have not been fully met, even now that the treatments have been completed. The plot is showing improved signs of recovery but it is still recommended that closures continue to allow for the plots to receive appropriate rest to allow for seeded species to establish root systems and communities.
2022: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial and drill seedings have not been fully met, a year after treatments have been completed. The plot is showing small signs of recovery but it is still recommended that closures continue to allow for the plots to receive appropriate rest to allow for seeded species to establish root systems and communities.

AIM Plot 05 was correlated to the R028BY028NV Sodic Terrace 8-10” P.Z. in former / Sacrobatus vermiculatus – Artemisia tridentata / Leymus cinereus (greasewood – big sagebrush / basin wildrye) vegetation community on a fan piedmont.
The Aerial Sage-grouse seed mix was comprised of Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis), Basin big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp tridentata), and western yarrow (Achillea millefolium var occidentalis).
Density Results
2020: The rehab objective of 1 native forb/m2 and 0.3 shrubs/m2 have not been fully met. No seeded species were observed though native regrowth of grasses were relatively abundant.
2021: The rehab objective as stated above was still not met. Seeded shrub density increased but was still not significant enough to meet the threshold and seeded forbs were again not present. Native regrowth of grasses was lower than in 2020 but shrubs were relatively abundant at 1.42/m2. While not meeting the objectives the plot is making progress towards eventually meeting them.
2022: The rehabilitation objective has still not been met. No seeded species were observed again. Native regrowth of grasses increased to 11.4/m2, the highest observed since monitoring began in 2020. However, native regrowth of shrubs and forbs both significantly decreased with no shrubs be present in the density frames.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2020: Foliar cover was moderately low at 26.7% with annual grasses being most dominant (16.0%) followed by perennial grasses (9.3%). Annual forbs were the only other indicator observed and was very low at 0.7% on the plot. Annual species outnumber their perennial counterparts and are slightly more dominant overall.
2021: Foliar cover was moderately low and decreased by 6% since 2020 at 20.7%. Annual grasses and annual forbs are now co-dominant at 15.3% each while perennial grasses decreased by 4% to 5.3%. The continuing dominance of annuals on the plot is of concern.
2022: Foliar cover increased significantly to 73.3% cover with annual grasses dominating at 2.0%, followed by perennial grasses (23.5%), and annual forbs (9.0%). Perennial forbs were observed for the first time though only at 0.5% cover. The annual species cover is still much higher than that of the perennial species and the continually drastically increasing cover of annual grass is very concerning for the health and rehabilitation of the plot.
Gaps and Erosion
2020: Gaps were low and nearly equally distributed across the different size ranges.
2021: Gaps increased from 2020’s observations, dominated by gaps >200cm at 54.9% total. While decreases in gaps could be a positive sign for soil stability the high presence of annual species on the plot indicate that the overall health of the plot is low.
2022: Gaps redistributed quite significantly since 2021. Much of the gaps that were in the >200cm size class appear to have been broken up into the smaller size ranges. Again, while filling in larger gaps can be a good sign of soil stability and increased plot health, the extremely high presence of annual grass is of great concern for the future health of the plot.
Species Richness
2020: Species richness was moderate at 18 individual species identified on the plot. Annual forbs and grasses outnumber their perennial counterparts.
2021: Species richness was moderate at 22 individual species identified on the plot. The number of perennial forbs and perennial grasses increased and now outnumber their annual counterparts.
2022: Species richness was moderately high at 25 individual species identified. Annual and perennial forbs had increases while perennial grasses lost two species. Despite these changes perennial species do still outnumber their annual counterparts.
Recommendations
2020: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial have not been fully met, although not all treatment was completed. Some seeded species have been observed and recovery of perennial species is apparent. There was a grazing closure issued for the Shafter fire area. It is advised that the fire area is reviewed and receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish.
2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial been fully met, even now that the treatments have been completed. Plots are showing signs of recovery but it is still recommended that closures continue to allow for the plots to receive appropriate rest to allow for seeded species to establish root systems and communities.
2022: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial and drill seedings have not been met, even now that the treatments have been completed and given at least a year to establish. The plot is showing minimal signs of recovery but particularly with the greatly increasing coverage by annual species observed, it is still recommended that closures continue to allow for the plots to receive appropriate rest to allow for seeded species to establish root systems and communities.

2020 was a difficult year due to the coronavirus and most notably the season started later than 
usual. This could show itself as an incorrect perennial species count due to many drying out

ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
S3 Aerial Chaining/Aerial Sage Seeding
Shafter Complex AIM Plots 04, 04A, and 04B were all located in a Forested PIMO-JUOS/ARNO4/PSSPS-ACHY site in a former Singleleaf pinyon-Utah juniper (Pinus monophyla-Juniperus osteosperma)/Black sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp nova)/Bluebunch wheatgrass-Indian ricegrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata-Achnatherum hymenoides) vegetation community on mountains.
The Chaining Mix was comprised of Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), Indian ricegrass (Achnatherum hymenoides), Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile), Antelope bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata), and Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium var occidentalis).
The Aerial Sage mix was comprised of Black sagebrush (Artemisia nova), Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis), and Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium var occidentalis).
Density Results
2021: The rehab objective of 1 native forb/m2 and 3 seeded species/m2 have not been met. Indian ricegrass was the only seeded species observed in the density plots and was observed on average 0.39/m2, not meeting the objective.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives as stated above have not been met. Many more perennial grasses were observed this year, Indian ricegrass, Sandberg bluegrass, Bluebunch wheatgrass, Squirreltail, and Siberian wheatgrass were all observed. Native regrowth of grasses and shrubs increased while forbs declined by nearly half.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2021: Average foliar canopy cover was extremely low at 1.34%. The only plants observed during Line-Point Intercept were “Dead Beyond Recognition” or cheatgrass and there were only a total of 6 hits observed.
2022: Average foliar cover increased from 2021 but was still very low at only 7.8% total. Annual forbs were most dominant at 4.5%, followed by annual grasses at 1.3% total. This is a slight shift from 2021 where annual grasses were most dominant follow by perennial grasses. The low amount of foliar cover present on these plots leaves them susceptible to invasive annual forbs and grass taking over the plots and outcompeting the small amount of perennials present.
Gaps and Erosion
2021: Corresponding with the very low percentage of total foliar cover the most frequently observed gap class size was >200cm at 97.08%. No data was collected about sings of erosion on the plots but it stands to reason that these plots are very vulnerable to wind and water erosion while the coverage and therefore stabilizing root systems are essentially non-existent across the plots.
2022: Gaps were still extremely dominant on these plots but with the slight increase in foliar cover there was a slight redistribution of gaps from the larger size ranges to the smaller ranges. Knowing the foliar makeup of the plots it will be important to make sure that the reduction of gaps is due to an increase in perennial cover and not annual cover. The presence of rills and waterflow patterns observed on each of the plots again leaves these plots susceptible to soil erosion and for invasive annuals to take full dominance across the plots.
Species Richness
2021: Despite the extremely low foliar cover species richness was only moderately low for these plots at an average of 17 species/plot. Perennial species on average did outnumber annuals due to perennial grasses but only Shafter Complex 04 perennials fully outnumbered annuals. The presence of trees and shrubs could help contribute to soil stability in the future.
2022: The average number of individual species identified across these plots was moderately high at 24/plot. Perennial grasses and forbs still outnumber their annual counterparts but given the foliar distribution of these species management will be needed to ensure the perennial species present can thrive across the plots.
Recommendations: 2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of aerial chaining/aerial sage seedings have not been met. It is strongly recommended that the closures of the Collar and Elbow pastures should remain in place in order to allow the area to receive proper rest and that seeded species may receive more time and opportunity to establish root systems and communities on site. 2022: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of aerial chaining/aerial sage seedings have not been met. It is strongly recommended that the closures of the Collar and Elbow pastures should remain in place in order to allow the area to receive proper rest and that seeded species may receive more time and opportunity to establish root systems and communities on site. Additionally, potential further treatments should be considered for these plots so that invasive annual species don’t spread and take over the entirety of the plots.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2022 MONITORING RESULTS
Monitoring plots on the Bishop Fire spanned 3 different Soil Map Units and 4 different Ecological Sites. Plots are in areas that had burned once or twice. Evidence of wild horses such as scat were observed by crews on 11 of the 12 sampled plots. Evidence of cattle was observed on just one plot (Table 3).
Following the second growing season, vegetation response is quite variable on the Bishop Fire. Invasive annual grasses, namely cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) are present throughout the A and C Seed Mix areas, but cover varies greatly. Cheatgrass is dominant only on plot BISH-CMIX-45 with 26% cover. Annual forbs are also abundant in some portions of the burn. The non-native prostrate pigweed (Amaranthus albus) is dominant in some areas of the burn, and native annuals fringed amaranth (Amaranthus fimbriatus), chinchweed (Pectis papposa) and ribseed sandmat (Chamaesyce glyptosperma) are common to dominant in some portions of the burn. The native annual grass sixweeks’ grama (Bouteloua barbata) was also common in the burned area. These annual species are establishing following the strong 2022 summer monsoon.

Resprouting shrubs are also common throughout much of the Bishop Fire. The ecological sites on the fire contain fire adapted species such as Sonoran scrub oak (Quercus turbinella), Desert
bitterbrush (Purshia glandulosa), desert almond (Prunus fasciculata), and desert ceanothus (Ceanothus greggii). These species were observed at covers from 4% to >10% on many of the plots. In the absence of repeat burning, these species could become dominant over time.
Perennial grass species, including those used in the A and C seed mixes are uncommon on the Bishop Fire. On all plots, perennial grasses had 2% total cover or less. Perennial forbs are common on the burned area, especially desert globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua) and whitemargin sandmat (Chamaesyce albomarginata). On three plots perennial forbs had > 10% cover.
The seeding objective of permanently establishing 15% desirable perennial plant cover on the burned area has been met on 3 of 12 plots and is close to being met on other plots. The A and C mixes on average contain 12.5% perennial cover. In the absence of future disturbance, it is anticipated that the 15% cover objective should be met.
The second and third objectives of the aerial seeding treatment are to establish one seeded species per square meter and 0.2 shrubs per square meter on average. Both of these objectives have been met following the second growing season post-burn for at least the A and C Mix areas (Tables 4 and 5). Additionally, the livestock closure objective of establishing 1-3 desirable perennial plants per square meter has been met on the low end in the A and C Mix areas with an average of 1.2 firmly rooted perennials per square meter (Table 4).

Objectives: The aerial seeding treatment will be deemed effective if the following objectives are met. 1) An average of at least 15% cover of desirable perennial plants permanently established in the burned area within two to five growing seasons post-fire. 2) The aerial seeding results in the establishment of 1.5 seeded species per square meter in the burned area. 3) Establish at least 0.2 shrubs per square meter in the seeded area.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2022 MONITORING RESULTS
After two growing seasons, the Baldy and Flat fires remain sparsely vegetated with only 16% total live plant cover on average (Table 3). Both non-native invasive annual forbs and native annual forbs make up the most common plant guilds with close to 10% combined cover on average. In some places (e.g. Baldy03) there are high covers of native annual plants. Crews were not able to identify many of the annual plants to species, and it remains unknown what native annuals were most common on the burn, but forbs were much more common than grasses. The warm season invasive Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) and the non-native mustard Descurainia Sophia were common non-native annual forbs. Cheatgrass is not abundant on the fire, with only 1% cover on average. There is no difference in cheatgrass cover on the plots applied with herbicide compared the plots not applied with herbicide. The plot with the highest percent cover of cheatgrass, Flat01 at 6% cover, was applied with herbicide. Perennial plant cover is low on the fire, and the first objective of the aerial seeding treatment to establish 15% desirable perennial cover has not yet been met. Green rabbitbrush (Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus) is one of the more common perennial shrub species on the fire. There are high covers of dead standing pinyon and juniper trees on the burn (not shown in table).

The second objective of the seeding treatments is to establish 1.5 seeded species per square meter on the burned area. This objective appears to be close to being met with an average of 1.3. Species used in seed mixes make up over 60% of the total perennial density on the burn. The objective of establishing 0.2 shrub species on average has been met, however, this is mainly due to one plot with an abundance of green rabbitbrush seedlings (Table 4).
Fifteen of the 23 species used collectively in both seed mixes were recorded on plots within the burned areas. Most seeded species are coming in at low abundance. The most common seeded species are Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) at 0.58 plants per square meter, Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda) at 0.3 plants per square meter and bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) at 0.11 plants per square meter (Table 5). More individuals of seeded species were identified as seedlings rather than survivors. The two species of beeplant used in just one mix were found at a higher presence in the seeded areas versus unseeded. The non-native species used in the mix including forage kochia, Siberian wheatgrass, and small burnet are establishing in many of these plots. These factors are all indicative of a seeding treatment effect. Only one species, desert globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua), is present at a similar frequency in the areas it wasn’t seeded versus the areas it was seeded. This is interesting because desert globemallow isn’t native as far north in Nevada as the location of these fires and could be a misidentification of a different globemallow species such as S. grossularifolia or S. munroana.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The Flat and Baldy fires have low total vegetation cover after the second growing season. The hotter and drier conditions during this time period are not conductive to plant establishment. Annual forbs (both native and invasive) are the most common type of plants on the burned area. A majority of the perennial plants establishing on the burn consist of species used in the seed mixes, and there is evidence to suggest that many of these species are establishing as a result of the seeding treatments.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2022 Monitoring Report
Following the second growing season, the Miller Fire remains sparsely vegetated with low total live plant cover (Table 4). Most of the perennial cover consists of trees and shrubs within unburned islands and strips present in the monitoring plots. The invasive annual cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was found on 9 of 10 plots but was found at very low covers (<1% on average). Observational notes from monitoring crews indicate that cheatgrass was patchy on the burned area. The invasive warm season annual forb Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) was also growing on 9 of 10 plots, but with higher covers than cheatgrass. Plots were monitored prior to the start of the strong 2022 summer monsoon, and it is possible that Russian thistle increased in abundance after the plots were sampled. An aerial broadcast herbicide treatment was applied to the burned area in September 2022, which will hopefully reduce the abundance of invasive annuals. Native annual forbs make up a significant group of plants on the burn, with species such as coyote tobacco (Nicotiana attentuata) common throughout much of the burn.

After two growing seasons, the Miller Fire has an average perennial plant density of 2.4 plants per square meter, and 2.0 firmly rooted perennials per square meter. This includes a balanced mix of grasses, forbs and shrubs. Close to 50% of the perennial plant density consists of species used in the three seed mixes.

The three most abundant seeded species are bottlebrush squirreltail, sandberg’s bluegrass and blue flax, which make up around 75% of the total seeded species density. All other seeded species were found at very low densities, or were clearly establishing via re-sprouting (e.g. serviceberry in Plot CMIX-24). Some species which weren’t used in all the mixes are also abundant in areas where they weren’t seeded, which is indicative of a natural regeneration effect rather than a seeding effect. This includes flat-bud prickly poppy and winterfat used only in the A Mix, which were present at 67% and 89% respectively of the nine plots in which they weren’t seeded. Some of the non-native species used in the mixes are starting to establish with moderate to high frequency and at low densities including forage kochia (90% of plots seeded), Siberian wheatgrass (50% of plots seeded), small burnet (67% of plots seeded) and sainfoin (33% of plots seeded). Hopefully with time and increased precipitation, these species can increase in abundance and out-compete invasive plants like cheatgrass and Russian thistle.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2022 Monitoring Report
Following the second growing season, the Miller Fire remains sparsely vegetated with low total live plant cover (Table 4). Most of the perennial cover consists of trees and shrubs within unburned islands and strips present in the monitoring plots. The invasive annual cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was found on 9 of 10 plots but was found at very low covers (<1% on average). Observational notes from monitoring crews indicate that cheatgrass was patchy on the burned area. The invasive warm season annual forb Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) was also growing on 9 of 10 plots, but with higher covers than cheatgrass. Plots were monitored prior to the start of the strong 2022 summer monsoon, and it is possible that Russian thistle increased in abundance after the plots were sampled. An aerial broadcast herbicide treatment was applied to the burned area in September 2022, which will hopefully reduce the abundance of invasive annuals. Native annual forbs make up a significant group of plants on the burn, with species such as coyote tobacco (Nicotiana attentuata) common throughout much of the burn.

After two growing seasons, the Miller Fire has an average perennial plant density of 2.4 plants per square meter, and 2.0 firmly rooted perennials per square meter. This includes a balanced mix of grasses, forbs and shrubs. Close to 50% of the perennial plant density consists of species used in the three seed mixes.

The three most abundant seeded species are bottlebrush squirreltail, sandberg’s bluegrass and blue flax, which make up around 75% of the total seeded species density. All other seeded species were found at very low densities, or were clearly establishing via re-sprouting (e.g. serviceberry in Plot CMIX-24). Some species which weren’t used in all the mixes are also abundant in areas where they weren’t seeded, which is indicative of a natural regeneration effect rather than a seeding effect. This includes flat-bud prickly poppy and winterfat used only in the A Mix, which were present at 67% and 89% respectively of the nine plots in which they weren’t seeded. Some of the non-native species used in the mixes are starting to establish with moderate to high frequency and at low densities including forage kochia (90% of plots seeded), Siberian wheatgrass (50% of plots seeded), small burnet (67% of plots seeded) and sainfoin (33% of plots seeded). Hopefully with time and increased precipitation, these species can increase in abundance and out-compete invasive plants like cheatgrass and Russian thistle.

Objectives: The aerial seeding treatment will be deemed effective if the following objectives are met. 1) An average of at least 15% cover of desirable perennial plants permanently established in the burned area within two to five growing seasons post-fire. 2) The aerial seeding results in the establishment of 1 seeded species per square meter in the burned area. 3) On average, at least 0.2 shrubs per square meter become established in the seeded area
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 11,176 acres would be aerially seeded with a mixture of perennial native and non-native grasses, forbs, and shrubs.
Actual_Implementation: The seed mix A was aerially applied to the 2020 Stewart Canyon Fire covering a total of 4,994 acres during the winter of 2020/2021. The helicopter seeded every other swath over the 4,994 acres for an approximate 2,497 seeded acres.\r\nDates and acreage verified by Seed Application Info document.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2022 Monitoring Report
Following the second growing season post-fire, the Stewart Canyon Fire is dominated by a mix of invasive annuals and native perennials, and in some areas native annuals are common (Table 4). Invasive annual grasses, namely cheatgrass, is most abundant in the higher elevations where the A Mix was applied. The invasive warm season annual Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) has become very dominant on the lower elevation west side of the burned area, especially in the B, C, D and E Mixes, with greater than 20% cover on eight plots. One plot, BISH-EMIX-57, appears to be located in an infestation of prostrate pigweed (Amaranthus albus) with 27% cover. The native annual rib-seed sandmat (Chamaesyce glyptosperma) is also abundant and dominant in some areas. These annual forbs are establishing following the wet summer monsoon in 2022, and monitoring plots completed in September/October are capturing this phenomenon.
Despite the dominance of invasive annual plants over much of the burned area, perennial plants, especially grasses and shrubs are regenerating well on the burned area. With over 20% cover of perennial plants on average within the burn, the first S3 Aerial Seeding objective of establishing 15% desirable perennial cover has been met. At the higher elevations, resprouting shrubs such as Gambel’s oak (Quercus gambellii), Sonoran scrub oak (Quercus turbinella), cliffrose (Purshia stansburiana) and desert bitterbrush (Purshia glandulosa) are common. Perennial grasses are common in much of the burned area, and on average make up close to 15% cover. At higher elevations, in mountainous areas, purple three-awn (Aristida purpurea), thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus), and crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) are abundant. At lower elevations on alluvial fan landforms, galleta grass (Pleuraphis jamesii) is common.
The second and third objectives of the aerial seeding treatment are to establish one seeded species per square meter and 0.2 shrubs per square meter on average. The first of these objectives have been met following the second growing season post-burn for the burned area as a whole (Table 5 and 6). The livestock closure objective of establishing 1-3 desirable perennial plants per square meter has been exceeded with an average of 3.5 firmly rooted perennials per square meter (Table 5). While resprouting shrubs are common and make up close to 5% cover on average, their densities remain low at a mean density of 0.082 plants per square meter. Since resprouting shrubs are often large, cover might be a better metric than density for reestablishment.
With an average of 1.4 seeded species per square meter, the objective of establishing one seeded species per square meter on average across the burned area has been met. This is due to primarily to perennial grass species, namely Siberian wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, thickspike wheatgrass, muttongrass, Sandberg’s bluegrass, and sand dropseed that all exceeded an average density of 0.1 plants per square meter. Most of the individuals recorded in the density frames were described as seedlings rather than fire survivors, indicating that they could be establishing from the seeding treatment. Interestingly, given the overall average density of 5.6 perennial plants per square meter on the burn, the perennial plant density objective would have been met without the seeding treatment. Of the 26 species used in the 5 seed mixes combined, 19 were observed in at least one plot and 7 of the species were observed on 50% or more of the plots. Some of the species with the highest average densities (e.g. Agropyron fragile, Elymus lanceolatus) were only found at 22% and 11% of the plots respectively, indicating that their establishment is limited across the entire burn, but these species are very abundant in the locations that they are establishing. Non-native crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) is common on some portions of the A Mix, which was not seeded as part of this project, is likely establishing due to the legacy treatment of the Non-Wilderness PJ Mix applied to the 2005 Delamar Fire, which overlaps with the A Mix.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2022 Monitoring Report
Following the second growing season post-fire, the Twin Fire is dominated by a mix of invasive annuals and native perennials (Table 5). Following a strong summer monsoon, native annual forbs, especially ribseed sandmat (Chamaesyce glyptosperma) are also abundant in many areas. Invasive annual grasses, namely cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) had greater than 20% cover on 9 of 25 plots, with an average cover of close to 18%. Cheatgrass was present on all plots. The warm season invasive annual forb Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) has become very abundant on two plots and is generally present throughout much of the burned area. Despite an abundance of invasive plants, the Twin Fire has had strong perennial recovery, with on average close to 15% perennial plant cover. This cover includes an even mix of perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs. There does not appear to be a negative correlation between invasive annual cover and perennial cover; perennials do not appear to be out-competing invasive annuals where they are establishing. Sites with high covers of perennials may also have high covers of invasive annuals. 

The objective of the aerial seeding and drill seeding treatments was to establish seeded species within the burned area. This objective appears to have been met, as seeded species were found on every plot, and on average make up greater than 60% of the total perennial plant density with 1.7 out of 2.7 plants per square meter.
While seeded species make up most of the perennial plant density on the Twin Fire, it is uncertain whether the establishing plants are from the seeding treatments or from natural regeneration. Crews make a distinction between plants establishing from seed (seedlings) versus resprouting and unburned (fire survivors) individuals, but this distinction is subjective. That some seeded species were only used in some mixes also allows for comparisons of their presence and abundance in areas where they were seeded and not seeded. For instance, the native forb Showy goldeneye (Heliomeris multiflorus) is a common fire follower species and was found more often in plots that it wasn’t seeded than where it was. Native perennial Galleta grass (Pleuraphis jamesii) was only seeded in the drill mix but was abundant throughout the burn and found at slightly higher average densities outside of where it was seeded (0.18 seedlings/sq m
and 0.15 survivors/sq m, data not shown in table). Most of the 31 species used in seed mixes collectively are showing up at very low densities or not at all. The most common seeded species that make up more than half of the seeded species density across all seed mixes are desert globemallow (Sphaeralcea ambigua) and bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides). Some species used in seed mixes are coming in at very high abundance but were not seeded across much of the burned area, e.g. muttongrass (Poa fendleriana) has a density of 6 plants per square meter but was only found in the one plot used for the 322 acre Aerial C Mix.

2022 Monitoring Report
Following the first full growing season, the Big Rocks Fire is dominated by invasive annual grasses, namely cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum). Cheatgrass cover is variable, ranging from 5% to 51% on the recent burned area (Table 4). Invasive annual forbs, especially Russian thistle (Salsola tragus) and tall tumblemustard (Sisymbrium altissimum) make up the second most abundant group of plants on the burned area. Perennial plant cover is quite low, with a combined average for grasses, forbs and shrubs of 5% on the burned area. A majority of the perennial plant cover consists of resprouting shrub species, especially desert bitterbrush (Purshia glandulosa), Nevada ephedra (Ephedra nevadensis) and green ephedra (Ephedra viridis).
The plots aerially seeded in the 2021 Big Rocks Fire, the natural regeneration plots, and the reference plots from the 2006 Hambly Fire all appear quite similar and consist of annual grass dominance, low covers of perennials, and resprouting shrubs. This finding is consistent with the 2016 ten-year ESR monitoring report for the Hambly Fire. Interestingly, the Big Rocks Fire has much lower perennial cover than the nearby 2020 Twin Fire (approx. 15% perennial cover on average) although both areas have reburned and primarily consist of the same Ecological Sites. Data collection on the Twin Fire occurred in September and October following a strong summer monsoon. Big Rocks data collection occurred prior to the summer monsoon in June.
The objective of the aerial seeding treatment is to establish seeded species. Following the 2022 season, one seeded species makes up most of the perennial plant density on the Big Rocks Fire. There are just over two perennial plants per square meter on average, and on the seeded plots, 1.8 plants per square meter consist of species used in the seed mix.
As with cover, perennial density between the seeded plots, the natural regeneration plots, and the previously burned reference plots are all quite similar. One minor difference is that perennial grasses are more common on the previously burned reference plots, and perennial forbs are more common on the Big Rocks plots (Table 5).
While seeded species make up the bulk of the perennial plant density on the Big Rocks Fire, it is unclear that their establishment is due to the seeding treatment versus natural regeneration. Twelve species were used in the Big Rocks Aerial Seed Mix. Five of these species were observed on monitoring plots (Table 6). None of the non-native species used in the mixes were observed by crews. Most of the seeded species seen were approximately as common in the areas they were seeded compared to the areas where they were not seeded. This is indicative of establishment via natural regeneration. There are two seeded species establishing at an abundance that is ecologically meaningful – desert globemallow and Sandberg’s bluegrass. Crews indicated that the Sandberg’s bluegrass establishing on seeded plots were fire survivors and not from the seed mix. This is a challenging distinction to make, especially for a small, shallowly rooted grass such as Sandberg’s bluegrass. Crews indicated that desert globemallow establishment was primarily from seedlings at an average density of 1.44 plants per square meter in the seeded plots. However, globemallow is abundant on both seeded and unseeded plots. Its mean density is essentially the same at 1.48 plants/sq m on the natural regeneration plots burned by the Big Rocks Fire, and lower at 0.41 plants/sq m in the reference plots not burned by Big Rocks Fire. Desert globemallow is a vigorous fire follower and is likely starting to fade out on the reference plots, which are now 16 years post-burn.
RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
Conditions on the Big Rocks Fire since its containment have been hotter and drier than normal. These conditions are generally not conducive to the establishment of seeded species. The Big Rocks Fire is dominated by cheatgrass, and perennial plant establishment is generally quite low. Most of the perennial plant cover on the fire consists of resprouting shrub species. The seeded species Desert globemallow is by far the most abundant perennial plant in terms of density, but it is found at a very similar density in the natural regeneration plots as compared to the seeded plots. This is indicative of a natural regeneration effect rather than a seeding treatment effect. Lastly, the Big Rocks burned area looks very similar to adjacent areas that burned in the 2006 Hambly Fire, and these areas look similar to how they looked in 2016 (See 10-year Hambly ESR Monitoring Report). This landscape appears to have experienced minimal change over time.

2020 Density Results: 
The rehab objectives of 0.3 native shrubs and 1 native forb per square meter has not been met for seeded species. However, seeded Wyoming big sagebrush and western yarrow were observed on the plots. Most of the grass regrowth was composed of Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda).
2020 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was moderate (32.8%) with Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) and cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) making up the majority of cover at 15% and 9.8% cover, respectively. Next most commonly encountered species were Squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) spiny phlox (Phlox hoodia) and tall annual willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum) at 2.8%, 2.0, and 1.7% cover, respectively. Perennial grasses and forbs collectively had more cover than annual species on the plots, indicating overall recovery in the monitoring sites.
Gaps and Erosion
Roads Complex AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland South Slope 8-12” P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia tridentata sbsp wyomingensis / Pseudoroegneria spicata ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass) vegetation community on the shoulder of a hill. Soils were determined to be 414 – Vanwyper-Loomis association (Vanwyper). No rills, gullies, or sheet erosion were observed on AIM Plot 01, although an common deposition/runoff, common pedestalling (with occasional root exposure), and moderately long, common water flow patterns were observed. This is a moderate departure of expected conditions on the R025XY015NV site, indicating some wind and water erosion.

Roads Complex AIM Plots 02 and 03 are located in a Rangeland Loamy 10-12” P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia tridentata / Pseudoroegneria spicata – Achnatherum thurberianum (/ big sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass – Indian ricegrass ) site on a fan piedmont. Soils were determined to be 414 – Vanwyper-Loomis association (Quarz) on both sites. No rills, gullies, deposition/runoff, or sheet erosion were observed on AIM Plot 02, although some pedestalling and water flow patterns were observed. No signs of erosion were observed in AIM Plot 03. These were a slight departure of expected conditions on the R025XY014NV site, indicating some water and wind erosion.
Roads Complex AIM Plot 04 is located in a Rangeland Loamy 8-10” P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia tridentate sbsp wyomingensis / Achnatherum thurberianum – Achnatherum hymenoides ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber’s needlegrass – Indian ricegrass) vegetation community on a floodplain/basin. Soils were determined to be 491 – Orovada-Puett association (Orovada). No rills, deposition/runoff, or sheet erosion were observed on AIM Plot 04, although an inactive gully, common pedestalling (with rare root exposure), and long, common water flow patterns were observed. These are a slight departure of expected conditions on the R025XY019NV site, indicating some water and wind erosion.
Approximately 63.4% of the transects had canopy gaps on the four plots. The most frequently occurring gaps were > 200 centimeters in length and these occupied 6.1 average meters (24.4%) of the 25 meter transects.
Species Richness: An average of twenty-seven (27.25) different plants species were observed within the four 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plots. AIM Plot 01 had twenty-one (21) species, AIM Plot 02 had thirty-four (34) species, AIM Plot 03 had twenty-six (26) species, and AIM Plot 04 had twenty-eight (28) species.

2020 S2 Drill and S3 Aerial Seeding, and S14 Imazapic Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial and drill seedings have not been fully met, although some seeded species have been observed and recovery of perennial species is apparent. There was a grazing closure issued for the Roads Complex fire area. The objective of three perennial grasses per square meter has been met (primarily through Sandberg bluegrass) in the aerial seeding and imazapic treatment areas but were not observed in the drill area.
